title: Iconographia Tychonis — Tycho Brahe's image and self-fashioning

images.label: The portraits on the equatorial armillary's pedestal
images.date: c. 1584 (instrument built) – Dec 1596 (the recording block's first issue); the inscribed '1580' is Tycho's floruit year, not an execution date
images.maker: Unrecorded. Christianson's 'probably painted by Gemperle' remains an uncited hedge (grade C) - Beckett & Christensen 1921 never mention these portraits, and DBL's Gemperlin entry is silent on the armillary. Gemperlin WAS available: recruited at Augsburg 1575, royal settlement letter 23 April 1577, documented in Denmark from 1578, died 1587 of a Copenhagen epidemic on Tycho's own printed testimony (De mundi II, p. 284) - his residency brackets the whole preferred painting window.

bounds.argument: Name-labels N·C·T·G / T·BR·D sit on the entablatures above the niches; the year-tablets on the plinths beneath the figures read '…520' (leading digit obscured by the block's own carved bracket in every impression examined) and '1580' ('I580' is the font's flag-serif numeral 1). The years are floruit labels, settled by direct inspection of Nathan Chytraeus, Variorum in Europa itinerum deliciae (Herborn 1594), pp. 596–598 (2026-08-03): the Stjerneborg hypocaustum cycle — Tycho's own sibling lineage programme, on material his preface says came largely from Tycho himself — gives every figure an 'Anno X' floruit line, with COPERNICUS 'Anno 1520 post Christum' and TYCHO BRAHE 'Anno 1580': the identical pair of years the pedestal tablets carry. The pedestal therefore uses the same convention (and the obscured '…520' is confirmed as 1520); '1580' cannot in any case date the execution, since no armillary existed then. Christianson 2000's reading of 1580 as a construction year (against his own 2020 chronology) is thereby retired; what 1580 commemorates within Tycho's career (Uraniborg's completion is Dreyer's candidate) remains open, and Zeeberg 1995 ('The Inscriptions at Tycho Brahe's Uraniborg', in Skafte Jensen ed., Odense 1995, pp. 251–66 — undigitized; online retrieval exhausted 2026-08-03) is now corroborative rather than load-bearing. If Christianson's hedged Gemperlin attribution were adopted, the upper bound would fall to 1587; it stays 1598 (publication of the recording plate). The 1585 Icones instrumentorum (Nielsen 976, Uraniborg broadsides, Marburg unicum - enclosed with Tycho's 1 March 1586 letter to Wilhelm IV) was checked as a possible earlier attestation (2026-08-04): its armillary woodcut depicts the STEEL armilla (Fig. 13 type; 'pes...ex solido metallo'), not this instrument - a diagnostic null that leaves the 1598 plate the earliest witness to the portraits. MOVED 2026-08-04: the hard upper bound advances 1598 -> December 1596 - the Icones instrumentorum suite (Nielsen 975, Uraniborg 1596, 18 letterpress-free woodcut pulls issued with some Epistolae copies; presentation copies to Christian IV and Chancellor Friis in December 1596) contains the armillary printed from what is almost certainly the same woodblock (Stockholm KB exemplar examined leaf-by-leaf: identical tablets, V-medallion, and the full compositor letter-key in identical positions; print-flaw-level confirmation pending an uncoloured 1598 impression). The painting window is therefore [summer 1584 -> Dec 1596], preferred sub-window 1584-87 unchanged. The block itself was cut somewhere in [1584 -> 1596]; the documented production waves (two blocks 1585, two 1586-87 for De mundi, several 1592-93 for the Progymnasmata, boxwood-only from April 1590) make the post-1590 campaign the likeliest home for it, stated as preference.

images.description: Four portraits were painted on the wooden pedestal of the smaller equatorial armillary — the instrument of the Mechanica's Fig. 12, whose pedestal Tycho describes as built 'e solido et forti ligno'; not the great steel-based armillary of Fig. 14, built later, whose chapter mentions no portraits. Tycho and Copernicus occupied the two visible niches, Ptolemy and Albategnius the hidden reverse. Tycho names them himself in the Mechanica: 'sunt 4. Icones … quae effigies Ptolemæi, Albategnij et Copernici; tum quoque NOSTRAM repræsentant' — and ours too. The instrument put him into the lineage physically, on the object that did the measuring. Blaeu re-engraved the whole plate on copper for the Grooten Atlas (Amsterdam 1664, Hven section): the pedestal programme is carried over intact - both niches with their figures, the plumb-bob cartouche, and the year-tablets, with '1520' engraved in full (the woodcut's carved bracket no longer obscures the leading digit) - while the right entablature is re-lettered 'T.B.N.D.' against the woodcut's 'T-BR-D' (engraver's error or a deliberate re-reading; which, is undetermined). Derivative of the woodcut rather than of the lost instrument, but the fullest posthumous transmission of the portrait programme. The instrument's place is settled from Tycho's own Uraniborg room-list (2026-08-04): 'S. Observatorium minus Septentrionale, alias Armillas AEquatorias continens num. 12' - the lesser NORTH observatory of the main house, with the steel sibling (Fig. 13) in the south room under key N; the house-key letters invert the compass sense, which also explains Blaeu's 'Armillae S' section heading. The same room assignment already stands in the 1596 Epistolae. The entablature initials follow the lineage formula of the sibling Stjerneborg headings (name + origin): T-BR-D = Tycho BRahe Danus (anchored by Chytraeus's 'Tycho Brahe Danus de Knudstryp'), N-C-T-G = Nicolaus Copernicus Torunensis G[ermanus] - the G a structural inference completing the Danus/Germanus pairing, nowhere spelled out. The tablets' years are round-decade floruit values like the whole Stjerneborg series (300 BC...1520, 1580); 1520 = Copernicus's Frombork observing maturity in Tycho's assignment; what 1580 commemorates stays open (Uraniborg's completion leads, per the Mechanica's own 'CIRCA ANNUM 1580' caption). Against Blaeu's re-lettered 'T.B.N.D.', the woodcut's T-BR-D governs: the lifetime block was cut under Tycho's control, and its crude period R invites exactly the misreading the 1664 engraver made. The block's first issue was not the Mechanica: the Icones instrumentorum suite (Uraniborg 1596, Nielsen 975 - bare image-pulls without letterpress, keyed to the Epistolae's instrument descriptions) already carries it, so the portrait programme is attested by December 1596. Four Icones copies are documented (Stockholm KB, Vienna, Wroclaw, and the Sophia Epistolae+Icones sammelband, stock 5766).
images.nature: The painted originals are DESTROYED with the instruments. What survives is the record: the Mechanica plate.

whereabouts.summary: Painted originals destroyed with Tycho's instruments at Prague. The plate survives in every intact copy of the 1598 Mechanica.
whereabouts.tier: destroyed (originals); located (the recording plate)
whereabouts.note: The Mechanica's instrument plates are woodcuts, not engravings — only six illustrations in the book are from copperplates. The pedestal plate is printed from the identical woodblock in the 1602 Hulsius reissue — the inscriptions are letter-for-letter identical; the one armillary re-engraved on copper in 1602 is Fig. 13, not this plate. Fate (2026-08-04): not among the four giant instruments left on Hven in 1597 (Tycho's own Wandsbek list, TBOO XIII.101-104), so it travelled with the general train, reaching Bohemia only in Oct/Nov 1600 (Dreyer p. 320; Thoren JHA 1973 via Wolfschmidt). After 1601 the accounts fork - most instruments confiscated toward Vienna by 1604 (Schuppener after Kleinschnitzova) vs. destroyed after the 1619 Bohemian war (Wolfschmidt) - unreconciled; no fragment survives (only the two NTM sextants survive of all the instruments). Bergeron's 1603 Belvedere ensemble (four rulers + four astronomers, matching Resen 1668) is a DIFFERENT programme from this pedestal's two-name scheme.

images.label: The Kronborg tapestry figure — the conjectured earliest likeness
images.maker: Hans Knieper's tapestry workshop, Helsingør (the royal genealogy series for Kronborg)

bounds.argument: The dating is the one certainty: the royal genealogy tapestry series for Kronborg was woven 1581–1584, so the figure — whoever he is — falls in that window on hard documentary grounds. Everything else is conditional: the identification as Tycho, first proposed by Wanscher (Kronborgs Historie, 1939; Mortensen's 'Kbh. 1930' is a probable citation error — Wanscher's 1930 book is Rosenborgs Historie), rests on facial resemblance in a small background figure and has never been proven ('possibly correct' was Mortensen's verdict). If the identification holds, this is the earliest surviving likeness of Tycho, made when he was 35–38.

images.description: In the great tapestry of Frederik II and the young Crown Prince Christian (IV), two small noblemen stand at a balustrade overlooking the Sound. The right-hand figure, facing the viewer, has since Wanscher (1939) been conjectured to be Tycho. Direct examination of the tapestry photograph at full resolution (July 2026) settled two points the literature left vague: the figure wears a soft beret with a jewelled band and a large white ostrich plume — a worn plumed hat — and around his neck three twisted chain strands, one carrying a round medallion on a link chain; no Order of the Elephant. That chain-and-medallion scheme matches both the young Christian IV and the candidate's own companion (identified in the literature as Gert Rantzau, lensmand of Kronborg) in the same weave — three figures carrying the same ornament, weighing toward workshop convention rather than personal insignia. It is tempting to date the figure by the absent Elephant, but the year Tycho received that order is nowhere documented and the usual 'c.1585/86' is itself inferred from portraits — so the costume corroborates the weaving date here rather than independently fixing anything. His companion leans beside an undetermined round object on the ledge — at full resolution it shows no meridian ring, banding, landmass, or stand, so it cannot be read as a globe rather than a hat, cushion, or plain ball. Taken together: if Wanscher's identification is right, a plumed-hatted Tycho image existed already in 1581–84, and the beret worn in the second de Gheyn engraving a decade later was a return to how he actually dressed, not an invention. That reading inherits the identification's conditional grade and cannot be pressed harder than it: the resemblance that suggests the identification cannot simultaneously prove the costume history.
images.image_credit: The conjectured Tycho figure (right) at the balustrade, detail from the Frederik II / Christian IV tapestry, Knieper workshop, Helsingør 1581–84. Nationalmuseet, Copenhagen.
images.nature: An original weaving of 1581–84 — its originality is not in question. What is conjectural is the IDENTIFICATION of the small right-hand nobleman as Tycho, first proposed by Wanscher (1939; Mortensen's '1930' a probable citation error) on facial resemblance in a background figure, and never established.

conflicts.question: Is the figure Tycho at all?
conflicts.positions: The 2006 book says 'må være Tycho Brahe' and Nationalmuseet's record says 'det må være Tycho Brache' — near-identical wording, i.e. ONE assertion from the owning institution, not two independent sources. Mortensen 1946 grades Wanscher's proposal only 'possibly right'.
conflicts.status: unresolved; grade C is correct and must not be upgraded on the 2006 book's authority

conflicts.question: Does the figure wear the Order of the Elephant?
conflicts.positions: Jern 1976 (p. 139, printed p. 142, n. 53) states the figure wears the Order of the Elephant ('behängd med elefantordén'). Wanscher's own text, quoted verbatim by Mortensen 1946, states the opposite: the figure still wears the golden chain with Frederik II's contrafej, the Elephant coming only in 1585 or 1586 — the Elephant's absence is in fact Wanscher's dating device. Direct image examination at full resolution confirms a round rosette-bordered medallion with no elephant form.
conflicts.status: resolved against Jern (paraphrase error — do not cite Jern 1976 for the figure's costume); residual: Wanscher 1939 pp. 64–65 remain unread at source

images.label: The Steensgaard panel — a lifetime portrait or an early copy, never tested
images.date: the likeness c. mid-1580s; the panel untested

bounds.argument: These bounds date the LIKENESS the panel carries, not the panel itself, whose status is genuinely open. The costume places the likeness in the mid-1580s: Tycho wears the Frederik II medal and not the Order of the Elephant. That argument is weaker than it looks and should not be leaned on hard — the year Tycho received the Elephant is nowhere documented (Friis: he must have had it from Frederik II, 'but when, or on what occasion, is not known'), and the usual 'c.1585/86' is itself inferred from portraits, so dating portraits by it is circular. What the panel plainly is not is a picture of the later Tycho: it shows neither the Elephant of the 1586–87 oil nor the stacked chains of the engravings.

images.description: A portrait of Tycho at Hvedholm and later Steensgaard on Funen, which Mortensen thought probably the oldest picture of him preserved in Denmark — while calling it 'en ældre Kopi', an older copy, and 'ikke godt malet', not well painted. Whether it is a lifetime portrait or a later copy has never actually been tested, and this record deliberately leaves it open. The copy reading is the standing position, but its evidential chain is one link long: Mortensen gives no basis for it; he had published the opposite in 1937, listing the same picture as the only 'Originalmaleri (?)' of Tycho preserved in Denmark; and two paragraphs after calling it a copy in 1946 he writes that it was 'painted in the mid-1580s'. The only earlier verdict, Friis's, is explicitly presumptive — he judged a different picture a copy and added that the same 'presumably' applied to this one, recording no examination. Against that, several things point toward a genuine picture of its period. Hvedholm passed in 1611 to Tycho's own brother Steen Brahe and stayed in Brahe hands until 1786, and the house held other dated sixteenth-century family portraits. The clumsiness is itself characteristic of the Danish and Scanian portraits of the 1580s. The composition matches no known print of Tycho. And most tellingly, the astronomical attributes — dividers, an armillary sphere with its meridian and great circles, a cross-staff — are restoration overpaint: strip them and nothing astronomical remains, only a plain Danish noble portrait in the standard formula of the decade. Someone assembling a 'Tycho Brahe' from the prints would have painted an astronomer; here a later hand had to add one. One physical detail appears in no publication: a 'T B' monogram in Roman capitals at the upper left, above the Brahe arms. Initials beside arms is a real sixteenth-century convention and equally what a later labeller would add, so it settles nothing — but it has been missed. Uniquely in his census, Mortensen records no dimensions, no support and no medium for this picture, so even 'oil on panel' is convention rather than attestation. The panel has not been traced since the Copenhagen auction that dispersed the Steensgaard contents (V. Winkel & Magnussen, 20 October 1938); no second, Hvedholm sale has been traced — the Hvedholm main building had passed to the state in 1928 and the contents most plausibly moved to Steensgaard with Hendrik Bille-Brahe-Selby. Mortensen's 1946 'at Steensgaard' repeats a location he had already published in 1937. The question is closable: every securely dated comparandum in this Danish group is oil on oak, so dendrochronology of the support would settle lifetime-versus-later outright.
images.image_credit: The Steensgaard panel, reproduced from Harald Mortensen, 'Portrætter af Tycho Brahe', Cassiopeia 8 (1946), facing p.57 — the only located photograph of the picture, and the sole surviving image record; the panel itself has not been traced since 1938.
images.nature: Open, and never tested. Mortensen called it 'en ældre Kopi' (an older copy) and 'ikke godt malet', yet in 1937 published the same picture as the only 'Originalmaleri (?)' of Tycho preserved in Denmark, and elsewhere dated it to the mid-1580s. No source records the panel's support, medium or dimensions, so no physical datum exists against which any candidate could be matched.

whereabouts.summary: Untraced since 1938 — but a strong candidate has now surfaced.
whereabouts.holder: Candidate: Det Nationalhistoriske Museum pa Frederiksborg
whereabouts.tier: untraced for the panel Mortensen photographed; the candidate A 8191 is itself located
whereabouts.note: The panel disappears after the 1938 Copenhagen dispersal of the Steensgaard contents following Hendrik lensgreve Bille-Brahe-Selby's death on 7 May 1938 (Danmarks Adels Aarbog 1985-87:561-23c, via finnholbek.dk I11378; danmarkshistorien.lex.dk gives 1937, carried as a flagged minority reading); the dispersal auction followed on 20 October 1938. Frederiksborg A 8191 — 'Ubekendt', dated ca. 1600, hanging in Stue 27, sitter recorded as Brahe, Tyge Ottesen — is a painting of exactly this type, and is the picture reproduced uncredited on the dust jacket of Tycho Brahes Verden (2006), whose source photograph Nationalmuseet credits to Frederiksborg.

conflicts.question: Is Frederiksborg A 8191 the Steensgaard panel?
conflicts.positions: FOR: the composition matches Mortensen's 1946 plate in every element — the T B monogram, the crest at upper left, the curtain ground, the meshed shoulder chain with a separate beaded centre chain, the Frederik II medallion, the armillary sphere and cross-staff at lower left, the object in the left hand. Frederiksborg's 'ca. 1600' is compatible with Mortensen's 'oldest picture of him preserved in Denmark'. Frederiksborg is the buyer one would expect at a 1938 Copenhagen dispersal of Danish historical portraits. AGAINST: the gap between inscription and crest, and the crest's size relative to the inscription, do not match the 1946 plate — a mismatch re-corroborated by direct re-inspection of the scale-matched composite built for the 2026-07-18 audit, and not dismissible as halftone noise (the foreshortening escape was tested and rejected). Two further findings cut against the identification without settling it: the moustache form of the Commons photograph groups with the original drooping (non-Hvidt) type — evidence against A 8191 being the 1937-photographed Hvidt copy, but non-diagnostic between 'is the Steensgaard panel' and 'is a further version'; and Karlson 1928 (note 24) attests a 1923 Hvedholm-to-Frederiksborg portrait transfer with copies substituted in place, keeping a 1923 arrival at Frederiksborg live as an alternative route.
conflicts.status: unresolved; the measurement against was re-corroborated on the scale-matched composite and is not dismissible as halftone noise, but it remains a photographic reading of a dirty, abraded picture and is not decisive either way

conflicts.question: Lifetime portrait or later copy?
conflicts.positions: Mortensen 1946 says 'ældre Kopi'; Mortensen 1937 published it as the only 'Originalmaleri (?)' in Denmark; Friis's copy verdict is explicitly presumptive ('formentlig') and extended by analogy from a different picture.
conflicts.status: open; closable only by examining the object — dendrochronology has never been attempted

open_questions: Ask info@frederiksborg.dk for A 8191's ACCESSION DATE AND PROVENANCE. An acquisition in or after 1938 from the Bille-Brahe-Selby dispersal would close the identification. A registry lookup, not research — the cheapest decisive step available, and now the ONLY accession channel: the KID/Kunstindeks Danmark route is a dead end (Frederiksborg is absent from samlinger.slks.dk's 134-museum roster, and an exact museum filter returns zero artwork records).

Harald Mortensen, 'Den ældste Tycho Brahe-portræt', Nordisk astronomisk tidsskrift n.s. xvi (1935), p.58 — never consulted by anyone in this programme. The title matches his superlative for this panel exactly, and it predates both his 1937 'Originalmaleri (?)' and his 1946 'ældre Kopi'. Digitisation routes are exhausted: ADS scan delivery is authentication-walled (its holding of the scan unconfirmed either way); Runeberg, tidsskrift.dk and Internet Archive are negative; the 1934 Norway companion piece, now recovered via nb.no, is silent on Steensgaard. Det Kgl. Bibliotek's reading room remains the only route.

The 1938 dispersal catalogue: a copy of Fortegnelse over indbo fra Steensgaard (V. Winkel & Magnussen, auction 20 October 1938) is purchasable from Gurra's Books, Hemse, item #026711, ~US$29 — a lot entry would give dimensions, support, attribution and the buyer. Precondition before it can serve as evidence: verify the title-page decedent — the bookseller's transcription reads 'Baron Preben Bille-Brahe-Selby' against the documented Hendrik lensgreve, most likely a transcription error, but not settled until the physical title page is seen. Det Kgl. Bibliotek's file copies (V. Winkel & Magnussen; Kunsthallens) remain the institutional check.
Verify Daniel Hvidt's two painted copies live: M/S Museet for Søfart, Helsingør, and the Astronomisk-Historisk Samling at Rundetårn. Both rest on Mortensen 1946 alone.

If the panel is located: dendrochronology, then infrared reflectography and X-radiography, to settle lifetime-versus-later and whether the astronomical attributes are restoration overpaint, as Mortensen suggested.

images.label: The Stjerneborg astronomer cycle — Tycho as the terminus of his own science
images.maker: Unrecorded. Tycho names nobody. Beckett & Christensen assume Tobias Gemperlin 'stiltiende' and attach the meteorological-diary painter entries of spring 1591 to this cycle — impossible, since Gemperlin was dead by 1587. No source documents any painter. Hans van Steenwinckel — documented at Stjerneborg's design and construction (c. 1584, resident on Hven through 1590) and as painter of the mural quadrant's perspectival architecture — is the best-profiled alternative, likewise unattested for this cycle. Christianson's Gemperle sentence restates Beckett (his entry cites Christensen & Beckett 1921, 18–21) and is not independent evidence.

bounds.argument: Stjerneborg was built in 1584, so nothing could be painted in its warming room before that. The completed eight-figure cycle, including the Tychonides panel, is described as painted — icons with gold-lettered distichs in the hypocaustum — in Nathan Chytraeus, Variorum in Europa itinerum deliciae (Herborn 1594), pp.596–598, on material Chytraeus's preface says came largely from Tycho himself; Tycho's own fuller printed description follows in the Epistolae astronomicae (1596). The painting campaign in the meteorological diary falls in spring 1591, inside the window but tied to this cycle by no source.

images.description: Painted above the carved cornice of the warming room at Stjerneborg: eight astronomers reclining in succession — Timochares, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, Albategnius, Alfonso, Copernicus, then TYCHO himself holding a painted slip lettered QVID SI SIC? ('what if thus?'), and finally an eighth figure named TYCHONIDES, a descendant yet to come. The dome above carried his own world system. It is the most explicit surviving act of Tycho's pictorial self-fashioning: he paints himself as the terminus of the entire history of astronomy and then adds an heir after himself. Resen 1668 (pp.344–345) additionally records, near the centre of the room in a separate space, a distinct vanitas composition — a laurel-crowned philosophising youth with celestial globe and book, opposed to Death guarding worldly treasure, under VIVIMUS INGENIO, CAETERA MORTIS ERUNT — not to be conflated with the Tychonides figure.
images.nature: Original wall painting, DESTROYED. No painted-plaster fragment is attested in the excavation literature (1823–24, 1901 — explicit published negative, 1902, 1924, 1951) or in the K-samsök federated heritage database (queried 2026-07-20); SHM's and DigitaltMuseum's own databases and the Tycho Brahe Museum inventory remain unchecked. The 1946 Lund jubilee 'Stjerneborg motto' wall decoration is a modern recreation, not a survival.

conflicts.question: Who is 'Tychonides'?
conflicts.positions: 'A still unborn … possible descendant' — Beckett & Christensen 1921. 'Tænkte arvtager' (notional heir), »Tychonides« in scare quotes — Zeeberg 1993, pp.18–21. 'The Tychonides, Tycho's male offspring' (literal but unspecific) — Mosley 2007, p.25. 'Dvs. Tychos søn' — Grinder-Hansen ed. 2006, flat exhibition caption, unargued. Textual anchors: the authorial 1596 print is third-person and nameless, and TYCHONIDES alone among the eight headings carries no floruit line (Resen 1668 p.343, page-image verified); the earlier Chytraeus 1594 state is first-person ('ipse & inibo vias').
conflicts.status: unresolved; report it as a patronymic figure read variously as the actual son or a generic heir

images.label: The Frederiksborg oil (attributed to Gemperlin) — known through C. A. Jensen's 1838 copy
images.maker: Attributed to Tobias Gemperlin (Augsburg painter in Tycho's service from 1575, dead of the Copenhagen plague by 1587). The attribution is scholarly consensus resting on the working relationship, not on a signature or document — and the hedge is foundational, not late: Friis ('vel det sandsynligste, at det har været et Originalportræt, malet af Gemperlin') and Madsen ('vel') both hedged it at the outset, and Mortensen and the Dansk Biografisk Leksikon hedge it still. Beckett's 1897 case compared Jensen's copy only to the 1586 engraving and a sketch then under Goltzius's name — derivatives to derivatives, never to the signed Vedel 1578 or St Ibb 1578 anchors — and Karlson (1928), who also showed that Beckett attributed Gemperlin works from reproductions, doubted the attribution in a single unreasoned clause judged 'efter kopian'. Hans Knieper is excluded as a rival hand by Tycho's own division-of-labour statement on the 1587 mural quadrant.

bounds.argument: The lower bound rests on Gassendi's report (1655 ed., p. 137) that toward the end of 1586 Tycho 'wished to be depicted' by Gemperlin — voluit, a volitional construction, not a flat report of a completed sitting; the 'fortieth birthday' precision sometimes attached to this is not in Gassendi's narrative but belongs to the caption of the volume's unrelated frontispiece print. The burned picture's own inscription, as reported by Friis (Bidrag til dansk Kunsthistorie, p. 229), 'Anno Domini 1587 aetatis suae 40', independently corroborates the 1586/87 window; a sweep of the TBOO correspondence for 1586–88 is negative. The Order of the Elephant the sitter wears supplies only a floor: Christianson (2020, p. 97) dates Tycho's grant to 3 May 1580 at Odense (quote verified; his footnote's archival source not yet traced), so the device gives a hard 1580 terminus post quem rather than a mid-1580s one. The upper bound is firmer: the painter's death. Tycho's own De mundi aetherei II (printed at Uraniborg 1587) records Gemperlin dead of the plague — so if the attribution holds, the panel cannot postdate 1587.

images.description: The best-regarded painted likeness of Tycho: a lost life-size half-length oil showing him bare-headed and near-frontal, the Order of the Elephant on a double gold chain, both hands on his chest, four rings (including his signet) on the left hand, and the Brahe arms in the upper corner. The artificial nose-bridge — Beckett noted it 'evidently slightly reddened' — is shown more clearly than in any other portrait. Mortensen (1946, p. 60) describes the false nose and a scar running from the right eye up over the forehead as two distinct, coexisting features, citing Sandblad (Lychnos, 1937) for the scar as a duel memento; Sandblad itself remains unread, and the scar is not resolvable in the available reproduction chain. How the painting entered the Karen Brahe / Odense Adelige Jomfrukloster collection has two candidate routes, neither archivally proven: direct Brahe-family descent (the route Schepelern and Bruun Hansen treat as more probable) or transmission via Tycho's kinsman Holger Rosenkrantz (Schepelern's secondary 'måske', resting on a Sophie Brahe correspondence, and asserted flatly by Christianson (2000, p. 120) without a footnote of its own); the one primary document, Tycho's letter of 10 July 1597, is read by Mortensen (1946, p. 23) as concerning the full-length exile-type portrait, not this panel — and Gemperlin was dead by 1587 in any case. The picture was transferred by royal order of 9 October 1838 to the portrait gallery at Frederiksborg, and burned there in the great fire of 16–17 December 1859. It survives through C. A. Jensen's 1838 oil copy (84.5 × 68 cm, now Roskilde Kloster — the image shown here) and H. V. Bissen's 1858 pencil drawing (Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek). How faithful is the copy? The July 2026 adjudication: highly faithful in iconographic content — Jensen preserved the unflattering specifics (the reddened prosthesis, the four rings) an ennobling copyist would suppress, Bissen's independent drawing agrees on the whole scheme, and Høyen, who saw the original at Odense in 1830 (his Notitsbog, per Beckett 1897; Bruun Hansen 2013, citing Schepelern pp. 37, 56), himself called it 'nobler in form' and more youthful than the prints — so the nobility was in the original, not added by Jensen. Only the surface handling is genuinely unknowable: no witness records the lost painting's brushwork, and Jensen's smooth Golden-Age finish is plausibly his own.

images.label: The woodcut 'Effigies' (Westergaard 1376) — the praedelineatum's record
images.maker: Anonymous cutter — Nielsen 1921 (p. 185) infers, from a 1585 letter and undeciphered monograms, that German wood-cutters resided at Uraniborg; no cutter is named for any Uraniborg block, and off-island cutting cannot be excluded (Tycho's wood-cutter was away in Germany, Aug 1585). After a model in the Gemperlin likeness family; that Gemperlin ever cut a block is explicitly not established. The Stenwinkel sketch attribution rests solely on an uncited sentence in Christianson 2000, p. 291.

bounds.argument: The lower bound is the inscribed design date — 'aetatis 40 … 1586' names the sitting/design year, tied to Tycho's 40th birthday in December 1586. The upper bound is documentary: the block was in use on the title verso of the Progymnasmata prospectus distributed with letters of 20 February – 22 March 1592. The physical cutting date is open anywhere between those bounds. The 1588–90 wood-cutter recruitment letters concern instrument figures, never the portrait, and cannot anchor the block; the 25 Aug 1585 Hagecius letter shows cutting capacity intermittent and partly off-island. Both de Gheyn engravings retain the 1586 tablet years later — in this family the inscribed date travels with the design, not the object.

images.description: The woodcut portrait of Tycho — four carriers reconciled (Nielsen's three plus the Copenhagen prospectus quaternion), of which two impressions are verified by direct examination (Copenhagen, Marburg); Berlin's carrier is extant, and the Königsberg copy was reported destroyed (Norlind 1970) — the starting point of the portrait campaign and the best record of the plain scheme Tycho himself wanted: a single modest chain, the beret lying on the parapet — the 'praedelineatum' against which he later judged de Gheyn's first engraving overloaded. Bareheaded, in an emblematic composition of aristocratic splendour; the suggestion that the composition was sketched by Hans van Stenwinkel the Elder rests on an uncited sentence in Christianson 2000 (p. 291). The heraldic error in the ancestral quarterings is object-verified on the Marburg impression — BELKER with a barry charge standing where Vasa belonged, and the spelling HONNER for the Rønnow quartering; it persisted, part-corrected, into the first engraving, and the full correction (STORMVASE) is documented on the second engraving only — the woodcut has no corrected state.

images.label: The Prague panel — Mortensen's Clementinum portrait

bounds.argument: The panel, painted on wood and held in the astronomical museum in the Clementinum at Prague, is unsigned and carries the same composition and the same inscription as the 1586 woodcut, so the two are certainly connected. Which came first is the question. Mortensen argued the panel is the woodcut's MODEL rather than a copy of it, resting chiefly on a detail of the hands: the painting shows two rings that the woodcut leaves out, and a copyist adds detail rather than removing it. If he is right the panel dates from about 1586 and is the closest surviving thing to the painted stage behind the whole print campaign; if he is wrong the panel could be considerably later. He was himself tentative, and the record follows him without asserting him. Two further limits now stand on that question. The ring count — the sole load-bearing evidence for the model thesis — is untestable at the surviving reproduction's confirmed native maximum of 2200 × 3190 px: two independent attempts left no countable ring bands on either hand, so Mortensen's evidence is currently unverifiable in either direction. And since the panel's existence is itself attested by Mortensen alone, the existence question is logically prior to the dating question.

images.description: A portrait of Tycho painted on wood, which Mortensen (1946) placed in the Clementinum's astronomical museum at Prague. His passage cites no source and uses no first-hand autopsy language, and no other record from Studnička's Prager Tychoniana (1901) to a dated 2026 sweep of the Czech collections portal corroborates the panel's existence. Its correspondence with the 1586 woodcut rests solely on Mortensen's five itemized points: the same inscription (position confirmed on the reproduction, text illegible), bareheaded with sparse hair (confirmed), the prosthetic nose indicated (claimed by him, not visible on the sheet), the Order of the Elephant on a heavy double chain (a chain is visible; single or double, and the pendant, are unresolvable), and the rings on the hands (untestable). The heraldic apparatus, which Mortensen never claimed as a correspondence, diverges in kind: a single mantled crest, not the woodcut's conserved arch of sixteen ancestral shields, and no beret is present. Mortensen read the panel as the woodcut's painted source rather than its descendant. It was reproduced as a photogravure by the Photographische Gesellschaft in Berlin — a sheet lettered 'Jeremias Falck sculpsit'. Genuine Falck engravings of Tycho exist — Rijksmuseum RP-P-OB-50.565 of 1644, Block 214 / Hollstein Dutch 214, described by Friis in 1890 and exhibited at the Rundetårn tercentenary in 1937 as W.1431 — so the lettering is not wrong for want of a Falck print of Tycho; it is judged erroneous because the sheet, compared at full native resolution, matches the located Falck engraving on no diagnostic point, and because its continuous painterly tonality is that of a reproduced painting rather than an engraving. A further, unlocated Falck plate is not formally excluded. Wellcome's own catalogue nonetheless titles the sheet 'Photogravure after J. Falck' (after Burgess 1973, no. 405.7). The image shown here is that photogravure sheet, and the identification of what it reproduces rests on Mortensen's description rather than on any inscription of its own: it matches him on publisher, on the Falck lettering, on reproducing a painting, and on the checkable points of his description, and faint lettering is visible at the upper left where he places the inscription. Not yet examined at object level in Prague, and no live Czech institutional record has been reached. Mortensen had, in 1942, dismissed two oil portraits at the Prague Observatory as worthless eighteenth-century copies after de Gheyn; he treats those oils and the Clementinum panel as separate objects but never reconciles the two accounts, and both stated locations trace to the same institutional complex. A third strand runs earlier still: Bergeron's 1603 account of the Belvedere memorial records two paintings of Tycho there, untraced after the collection moved in 1635 (Fučíková 2002) — lost painted Tychos in Prague are multiply attested, a base rate that fits several distinct objects and anchors none of them.

images.label: The mural quadrant portrait (Uraniborg)
images.fate: the painting lost with Uraniborg; survives only in the Mechanica engraving
images.maker: Tobias Gemperlin (figure) and Hans van Stenwinkel the Elder (architecture), both named by Tycho in the Mechanica; Hans Knieper (landscape) — Tycho names only 'Johannes of Antwerp, royal painter at Kronborg', and the Knieper identification is uncontested scholarship (Friis; Christianson 2000)

bounds.argument: The great mural quadrant itself was built in 1582 — nothing could be painted in its arc before that. The date 1587 is not merely conventional: it is inscribed on the plate's own tablet ('A° DOMINI 1587 ÆTATIS SVÆ 40', confirmed letter-for-letter at 600 DPI in two independent KB Copenhagen copies), and Tycho's text endorses the tablet ('prout vides'). The cap on Gemperlin's share of the work comes from his death — dead by 1587, the die-window running 1586 to May 1588 — not from Tycho's testimony. For the effigy and the architecture the attribution rests on Tycho's own word: he named Gemperlin and Stenwinkel outright, and praised the likeness in the Mechanica ('vix similior dari possit' — scarcely could a more faithful one be made); the landscape hand he named only as 'Johannes of Antwerp, royal painter at Kronborg', the surname Knieper being inherited, uncontested scholarship. A genuine late-1586 strand — Gassendi (via Resen 1668, attached to this mural effigy specifically), Thoren 1990, and Friis's earlier essay ('omtrent 1586') — dates the execution to late 1586; under aetatis-40 reckoning (Tycho's 40th year ran 14 December 1586 – 13 December 1587) both dates are consistent with a sitting late in 1586 completed by 1587.

images.description: Painted in 1587 within the arc of the great mural quadrant: a trompe-l'oeil 'diorama' in which Tycho, seated life-size in effigy in a fur-lined robe whose front carries a gold frog-and-button closure — no order insignia or pendant of any kind — looks up and points to the real observing-slit cut in the room's south wall, a dog (fidelity) at his feet and an open book with dividers and square on the table before him. Through the illusory wall one sees into the three storeys of the south tower — the vaulted laboratory, the library with the great brass globe, and the observatory with working assistants — flanked by medallion portraits of Frederik II and Queen Sofie; a tablet records it as the work of Tycho, 'author of the building and the astronomical instruments', in his 40th year. The painting perished with Uraniborg and survives through the copperplate engraving in the Mechanica (1598); a re-cut woodblock derivative of the plate appears in the 1666 Historia Coelestis (Liber Prolegomenon, p. cxiii).

images.label: The gilt portrait supralibros — two dies
images.maker: Cutter unrecorded. With the die now dated before late March 1588, Gemperlin (dead by 1587) is possible as designer and Hans Crol, Tycho's goldsmith on Hven (d. 30 November 1591), as cutter — but these are names of convenience, neither documented. The die pair's relationship is genuinely open: 1597 is the small die's first documented use, not a cutting date. If it is a later cutting it needs another hand; but Friis (c. 1890) held the small die the OLDER of the pair — undefended, and the shared design cannot by itself discriminate one commission from two cuttings off one pattern.

bounds.argument: The upper bound is an object: the Royal Library's Sascerides copy of De mundi aetherei (LN 428 4°, eks. 1) carries BOTH gilt ovals — portrait on the front cover, arms on the back — on its original parchment presentation binding, with Tycho's autograph dedication to Gellius Sascerides dated 20 March 1588 (verified on the EEB surrogate), so both dies existed by that date. The British Library's Maestlin copy, dispatched from Uraniborg on 14 May 1588, remains the second keystone — nobody rebinds a book INTO a Tycho presentation binding. The lower bound is the costume it carries: the multi-chain-and-medallion scheme belongs to the likeness layer begun with the 1586 sitting. This dating overturns the older literature's assumption (Mortensen; Christianson) that the stamp copies de Gheyn's engraving — the engraving was cut only in autumn 1590, two years after the die was in use. The small die's own first anchor is much later: its documented carrier is the Calvin/Theocritus volume Tycho gave Hans Lindenov, registered at Uraniborg on 21 March 1597.

images.description: Tycho's most personal device: a gilt-stamped portrait of himself, bust-length in a cartwheel ruff, wearing the loaded chain scheme of his royal favour — the Frederik II medallion with the initials F.S., an elephant pendant (the Order of the Elephant insignia — so read by Danske Magazin 1746, the earliest eyewitness, and by Mortensen 1946 on the model engraving; the photographs alone cannot resolve it), and a third chain whose ornament no witness has made out. Impressed in gold on the front covers of deluxe presentation bindings (the arms stamp on the back), it branded his gifts with his likeness: on De mundi (1588), the Epistolae (1596), the Mechanica (1598), and on Prague bindings to c.1601–03. Around the portrait runs the motto 'Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat, quae latet interior' ('here is Tycho's outward form; may the inner, hidden, shine more beautifully'). The stamp exists in TWO sizes, but the published metrology is shaky throughout: Mortensen 1931 prints the figures as '7,6 X 5,8 og 5,9 X 4,3 mm' — millimetres where centimetres must be meant, and with the small die's width drifting between 5.9 and 5.8 across his 1931 and 1966 articles; Friis (via the 1746 Lode plate's claim to render the stamps at their own size) gives 8 × 6 cm; a scaled estimate from the Stockholm RAR: 106 A digitisation (c. 6.3–6.5 × 5.9 cm) matches none of them; and every figure is taken from impressions on compressible supports, never from tools; the smaller die is far the rarer — its documented carrier is the KB Calvin/Theocritus volume given to Hans Lindenov — and it differs tellingly from the large: the small die's ruff edge carries serrated notches, rendering the lobed cartwheel ruff of the engraving family faithfully, where the large die smooths them away (Mortensen noticed the notches; object photographs confirm them). Two facts anchor the die pair's place in the story. First, the large die is the EARLIEST WITNESS of the multi-chain-and-medallion costume — it predates de Gheyn's first engraving, and on the leading reconstruction the costume scheme travelled from Denmark to the Amsterdam workshop, plausibly with the De mundi presentation copies in the hands of Heinrich Rantzau, broker of the engraving commission. Second, the dies were never revised: after the second engraving corrected the costume (c.1595), the binding stamps went on impressing the old loaded scheme for the rest of Tycho's life and posthumously — the correction was aimed at the print's public circulation, not at the livery of his bindings.
images.census_copies: PORTRAIT supralibros documented on: the KB Sascerides copy (LN 428 4°, eks. 1, autograph dedication 20 March 1588 — now the earliest dated carrier), the BL Maestlin De mundi (dispatched 14 May 1588 — the second dating keystone), the Magini De mundi, KB LN 428 copy 2, the Stockholm KB De mundi (RAR: 106 A), the Strahov Mechanica (green satin), the Wolfenbüttel Epistolae (HAB Astronomica 8), the St Petersburg Otto Brahe Mechanica (dedicated 5 October 1598), the Cambrai Lobkowitz Mechanica (dedicated 18 August 1600), and posthumous bindings to c.1603. NOT the Smithsonian Epistolae, whose cover carries the ARMS stamp.

images.label: Frederik II's funeral procession, 1588 — Tycho among the coffin-bearers
images.maker: Frans Hogenberg and Simon Novellanus, Cologne; commissioned by Heinrich Rantzau.

bounds.argument: Frederik II died on 4 April 1588 and the procession to Roskilde took place on 5 June; the engraved suite is dated 1589.

images.description: The engraved suite of Frederik II's funeral cortege. Tycho is said to have walked as number 7 in the left-hand row of the 32 bearers, between his brother Knud (no. 3) and his future brother-in-law Erik Lange (no. 11) — though the plate legend has the nobles bearing the canopy (tentorium) over the bier, not the coffin itself; 'bore the coffin' is the 2006 caption's compression. This would be the only documentary depiction of Tycho taking part in a Danish state occasion during his lifetime — he was 41 — but his physical presence at Roskilde on 5 June 1588 is unestablished: the Uraniborg diary notes 'Sepultura Regis' with no travel note for Tycho, against its own convention of logging his journeys.
images.nature: An original engraved suite. But this is a POSITIONAL claim, not a likeness — and the position itself is fragile. Direct full-resolution examination of the Kiel sheet (Yb 54-15) found no numerals and no name-list on the plate face, only the sheet number '15' and two royal captions; the legend 'Tentorium supra funus extulerunt nobiles sequentes' with its name column ('Canutus Brahe' legible; 'Tycho' never yet recovered from it) appears in the impression the 2006 volume photographed (Det Kongelige Bibliotek) and cannot currently be located on the Kiel sheet. The numbering's period basis is unestablished, and the 2006 book itself says outright that he cannot be picked out in the picture — 'uden at man dog sikkert kan udpege ham på billedet'.

Det Kongelige Bibliotek holds Rantzau's hand-coloured presentation copy to Prince Christian (IV) — the impression the 2006 book photographed, though which object that photograph actually reproduces is now an open question (see conflicts). Three presentation copies carry Rantzau gift-inscriptions dated 15 May 1590: Manderup Parsberg's (later Thore Virgin, Bibliotheca Qvarnforsiana, Uppsala 1946, no. 41; current whereabouts unknown), Christian IV's, and Duke Hans den Yngre's (Ilsøe, Fund og Forskning 44 (2005), p. 505, reviewing Zeeberg). Tycho's own copy was sent to him by Rantzau at the end of 1588 together with Civitates Orbis Terrarum Liber IV (Grinder-Hansen 2006, p. 222). Zeeberg's Rantzau bibliography deliberately excludes the Res gestae as a pure picture series ('ren billedserie') — which is why no numbered bibliography assigns it a number.

images.label: De Gheyn's first engraving (Westergaard 1377) — the 'overloaded' portrait
images.maker: Jacques de Gheyn II (Antwerp 1565 – The Hague 1629), signed in the plate; an independent Amsterdam engraver by 1588, previously trained in Goltzius's Haarlem workshop. No document names Goltzius anywhere in the commission — the old account that the commission 'went to Goltzius, who passed it to his pupil' is Beckett & Christensen's 1921 conjecture, built on premises (a dependent pupil; engravings of 1586) that are both refuted.

bounds.argument: The tightest-dated object in the whole series, on Tycho's own letters: 'nuper Amsterodami cupro insculptae' — recently engraved at Amsterdam — he wrote on 1 December 1590, dispatching impressions to Thomas Savile, with further sendings to Rantzau (7 December) and Scultetus (8 December). The letters name no artist; the plate is signed by de Gheyn. The inscribed 'aetatis 40 … 1586' names the likeness's origin, not the plate's date.

images.description: The first copperplate portrait: Tycho bareheaded within a triumphal arch of sixteen ancestral quarterings, the beret lying on the parapet, wearing the Frederik II portrait-medal and stacked chains — the loaded scheme the gilt binding die had carried since 1588. Whether that scheme reached the plate as an image transmitted from Denmark (plausibly with the De mundi presentation copies Heinrich Rantzau held) or was composed in Amsterdam under de Gheyn's documented house procedure — the model supplying the head, with costume, frame, arms and lettering engraved directly into the plate — is undecided; the commission's route is likewise unattested: Beckett & Christensen's 1921 conjecture that Rantzau brokered it has no documentary support and was never adopted by the print literature. Tycho reacted at once: on 7 December 1590 he complained to Rantzau that the portrait was overloaded with chains ('nimiis monilibus onustae') against the plainer model he had supplied, and ordered a replacement the same day. Forensic registration of impressions (2026) proved that the state-I and 'Marco Sadeler excudit' impressions in the Rijksmuseum are pulls of one plate — the Sadeler impressions are posthumous restrikes, not a new plate, the plate itself having passed to the Sadeler publishing stock from Tycho's estate. Whether the large-format impression printed integrally in a Copenhagen 1602 Progymnasmata copy and the smaller SMK impression come from that same plate remains open, awaiting plate-mark and raking-light comparison (a three-witness flaw comparison was negative but non-diagnostic, and water-staining of the Copenhagen leaf offers a paper-distortion alternative for the size differential). That 1602 title-verso impression is the engraving's only physically verified book use; the portraits found in five examined digitized Epistolae astronomicae copies are all the second engraving, to which New Hollstein assigns the Epistolae use — the insertions were loose, so copy-level variation among unexamined copies is not excluded. The plate carries the heraldic errors later corrected in the second engraving — BELKER standing where the Vasa sheaf belonged, HØNNOR for Rønnow — a list the 2026 shield-by-shield re-examination confirms complete at three (the VLFSTANDER, HØNNOR and BELKER shields; the thirteen others identical in both states) — and no depiction of the nose prosthesis or of any duel scar. The cartouche wording also separates the two engravings even on low-resolution digitizations: 'Machinarumque … Dispositarum' here, 'Instrumentorumque … Dispositorum' in the second plate.

images.label: The Copenhagen pen drawing (SMK KKSgb5254) — the second engraving's production drawing
images.maker: Jacques de Gheyn II is the best-supported hand (the pen medium is his documented practice for portrait-print models — 'Goltzius never did' so, per Reznicek — and the sheet's idiom matches his secure Marnix model); a residual alternative is an unidentified copyist supplying the model. Tobias Gemperlin is excluded as draughtsman (dead by 1587, and no secure Gemperlin drawing exists to compare). The old Goltzius attribution is refuted for authorship (no Tycho in Reznicek's corpus, wrong medium, Goltzius in Italy from late 1590); its documentary trail is a pre-1890s common opinion — still the museum's displayed label in 1921 — revived by Mortensen 1946 on the strength of a verso mark first recorded that year (Mortensen: the NAME Goltzius; Altena/SMK: a red-chalk 'HG' monogram) and judged forged by both the museum and the de Gheyn catalogue.

bounds.argument: The drawing is the working model for the second engraving — mirror-reversed against the print, needle-traced for transfer, the head at 1:1 with the engraved head (measured) — so it postdates the 7 December 1590 order for that engraving and predates the plate's completion, which Lambert Cornelisz's dated 1595 copy places by mid-1595. The 'ca. 1586?' sometimes attached to it is back-dating driven by the untenable Gemperlin attribution; the sheet's design CONTENT (the 1586 likeness of the 40-year-old) is older than the sheet. A residual alternative — one c. 1590 sheet serving both plates, v1's head also transferred from it — remains live and unexcluded: both engravings carry the identical AETATIS-40/1586 caption, and the documented v1→v2 manner shift (dense/tonal → lighter/linear) could make a single model read smoother in v1 and more furrowed in v2. The drawing's v2-matching age signature and worn cap are supporting but confounded observations (low–medium); the discriminating test — calibrated 1:1 scale registration of the head against NH 238 — has not been run.

images.description: The only early production drawing of the Tycho portraits to survive: pen and brown ink, 122 × 91 mm, bought by the print cabinet in 1810 from the heirs of Lorenz Spengler. Tycho in the worn plumed beret, head finished in disciplined engraving-idiom hatching, costume summary — exactly the workshop method (the model supplies the head; the rest was engraved directly on the plate). It is the mirror of the second engraving with the head transferring at 1:1: the physical signature of a sheet traced face-up onto the copperplate. Its costume differs from BOTH engravings (a taller plumed hat, an open radiating collar, two chains), which rules out every copy-after-print pathway — a copyist reproduces his source's costume. The lost companion design for the FIRST engraving is recorded by Altena (his cat. 653). The verso carries an old ink 'Thicho Brahe' inscription and the faint red-chalk 'HG' monogram that both the museum and the de Gheyn catalogue judge forged. The Goltzius attribution's documented trail is: the pre-1890s common opinion (Friis records no verso inscription at all, only the Spengler stamp), the museum's own Goltzius display label in 1921 (Beckett & Christensen, who argued instead for Gemperlin), Mortensen's 1946 report of the name Goltzius on the verso, and Altena's 1983 'false monogram HG'. Whether Mortensen's 'name' and the modern 'HG' initials describe the same physical mark is unresolved; a documented parallel for such an upgrade exists (the collector Ploos van Amstel added exactly such a false 'HG' to de Gheyn's Grotius drawing to sell it as Goltzius).

images.nature: An original working drawing — the only early production drawing of the Tycho portraits to survive.

images.label: De Gheyn's second engraving (Westergaard 1394) — the corrected portrait
images.date: ordered Dec 1590; design fixed by mid-1595; plate completed by 1596
images.maker: Jacques de Gheyn II, signed in the plate ('Geyn. fe').

bounds.upper: mid-1595 (design attested in Tycho's hands via the Cornelisz copy); plate completion by end 1596 (Altena's outer bound)
bounds.argument: The lower bound is Tycho's own re-order in the complaint letter of 7 December 1590 ('aliam illic confieri curem' — I am having another made there). The upper bound (revised July 2026): Lambert Cornelisz's reversed copy of this portrait is dated 1595 in its plate and was in Tycho's hands by 5 September 1595 (his letter to Pontanus) — so the design existed by mid-1595. Whether Cornelisz copied the printed plate or the Vorlage drawing KKSgb5254 is contested (Mortensen 1946 p. 21: 'Forlæg: Pennetegningen'); the 1595 date therefore pins the design with high confidence and the plate's completion only probably — the hard ceiling for the finished plate is Altena's 'before the end of 1596'. This still retires the older account that dated the model-delivery to May 1596 (the painter in Tycho's diary on 4 May and Blaeu's departure on 24 May 1596 cannot explain a design that was already circulating in Cornelisz's copy the year before). The corrected heraldry gives an internal lower bound as well: the error-state was still circulating on the February–March 1592 prospectus, so the correction falls between 1592 and the plate's completion (by end 1596).

images.description: The corrected replacement, and the portrait by which Europe knew Tycho: aged now, in the worn plumed beret, within the reworked arch. A complete change-register against the first engraving (22 verified differences, July 2026) shows a deliberately corrective new plate: the Frederik II medal removed and the stacked chains reduced to a single doubled chain (executing the 1590 complaint), the collar changed from standing to flat, the doublet opened — the whole dress more modest; the heraldic errors fixed (RØNNOR corrected, the Vasa wheat-sheaf cut where BELKER's bars had stood); the tablet's vocabulary revised from 'machinarum' to 'instrumentorum'; the sitter's face updated to the man of nearly fifty while the tablet keeps 'aetatis 40 … 1586', the caption of the likeness's origin; the hands transposed left-for-right while the head is NOT mirrored — the fingerprint of a freshly drawn plate, produced from the surviving Copenhagen drawing by direct needle transfer. The ornate pendant jewel over an elephant form survives from the first plate — the one costume element never revised. The plate faced the 1596 Epistolae; the engraving is recorded present in a documented copy of the 1610 Frankfurt-titled reissue (Amsterdam UvA OG 8°-2(1)), but that issue is unsold 1596 sheets under a new title-leaf — no fresh 1610 press-run of the plate is evidenced, and the Hülsius/Tampach lineage's documented portrait supply was a copy plate.
images.census_copies: Four digitised copies autopsied across all three issue-clusters (2026-07): every portrait present is the hatted second engraving — Smithsonian/Dibner (1596 issue, hand-coloured), ETH Zürich (1601 Hülsius issue), Florence BNCF (1610 Tampach issue); the Dresden SLUB 1610-issue copy lacks the leaf entirely (loose inserts do go missing). Nielsen §430 names no state ('et kobberstukket Portræt'). No copy carrying the capless first engraving has yet been found (n=4 of 29 census copies).

images.label: Lambert Cornelisz's print (Westergaard 1409) — the copy Tycho disliked
images.maker: Lambert Cornelisz (Amsterdam engraver of portraits and title pages, active 1593–1621 per CERL cnp02079345, which records 'Cornely' among his attested name variants and de Gheyn II as his teacher); the reproduced untrimmed impression carries a legible 'L Corney … fecit'; Friis's 'Cornay' is a contemporary 1868 note on a Vienna impression published 1902, and Mortensen's 'Cornely' derives from Friis's reproduction of the signature-less Copenhagen exemplar, not an independent reading; made on the engraver's own initiative, not commissioned by Tycho.

bounds.argument: The plate carries its own date, 1595, and Tycho's letter to his former assistant Pontanus, written at Uraniborg on 5 September 1595, shows he had already received impressions — one had come earlier via Cort Aslaksson, who wrongly believed it engraved at Cologne. The letter is also the print's significance for the whole chronology: being a reversed copy of the second de Gheyn portrait, its date proves the v2 image existed in copyable form by mid-1595; it dates the finished v2 plate only on the leading (unproven) reading that Cornelisz copied a printed impression rather than the design — the diagnostic zones are unusable because Cornelisz replaced the background apparatus, the mirror evidence is mixed, and CERL records de Gheyn II as his teacher (undated), a possible access route to pre-plate material. Under the design-model reading the plate's own terminus loosens and the May-1596 Blaeu/Pictor channel reopens.

images.description: A small Amsterdam trade engraving: Tycho bust-length in the plumed beret within an oval inscribed 'TYCHO BRAHE OTTONIDES DAN. ASTRONOMOR HVIVS SÆCVLI PRINCEPS 1595', his hand resting on two celestial hemispheres with a small armillary sphere between them — the engraver's own additions to a reversed copy of de Gheyn's second portrait. Tycho neither ordered nor liked it. His 5 September 1595 letter objects to the hemispheres ('Non satis placet, quod duobus hemisphaeriis imaginem istam inniti fecerit artifex' — it has less gravity) and to the epithet 'Princeps astronomorum' as too pompous an honour — but says not a word against the hat: the same editorial control he had exercised over the chains in 1590, tacitly accepting the hatted scheme. The print is rare; no institutional impression could be enumerated online in this programme, and the recorded apparatus is the Danish catalogue (Westergaard 1409), the descriptive primary account in Friis, Bidrag til dansk Kunsthistorie, p. 228 (the Kunstindustrimuseet impression, 9.2 × 7.8 cm, trimmed with the signature cut away; the 1868 Vienna sighting noted as 'L. Cornay'), and the trimmed reproduction in Friis 1902 (Nogle Efterretninger, per Mortensen).

images.label: The 1595 portrait medal — the only likeness in metal

bounds.argument: The medal dates itself: the obverse legend reads 'EFFIGIES TYCHONIS BRAHE O F ... AETATIS 49' and the reverse carries the date 1595 beneath the Brahe arms — Tycho was 48 turning 49 that year. Whether it was struck in his lifetime is a separate and softer question, and the hedges have three distinct roots: Dreyer's 'it has been suggested' derives from — and truncates — Danske Magazin II (1746), pp. 166–168, whose editors offered an explicitly unprovable twin conjecture (the completion of the star catalogue and the great brass globe reaching usable form in 1595); Beckett's suggestion that Tycho gave the medal as a princely favour is independent of that, from a 1946 private letter to Mortensen, not derived from the 1746 discussion; and the 1746 editors also floated Tycho's nephew Tage Ottesen Tott, then 15–16, as a possible commissioner. No contemporary document of 1594–97 attesting the medal has been found in the material searched. So the object and its date are documented; the lifetime striking is a reasonable inference, not a documented fact.

images.description: The one portrait of Tycho in metal, and the only one that carries his motto as its whole reverse design. It exists in two variants — a larger of about 39 mm inscribed with the verse 'Arma, genus, fundi pereunt; durabile virtus et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent' (arms, lineage and estates perish; virtue and learning hold nobility's lasting honour), and a smaller of about 35 mm inscribed simply 'ESSE POTIVS QVAM HABERI', to be rather than to seem. Both show a bearded bust in a ruff, wearing the Order of the Elephant on a double chain, on the obverse, and the Brahe arms with the date on the reverse. The maker is unknown, and Mortensen noted that the portrait matches none of the established painted or engraved types — it may descend from a likeness now lost. His verdict, though, is undefended — no comparison is shown — and the medal's costume, the Elephant on its double chain and nothing else, matches his own description of the pre-1590 lineage of the Clementinum painting and the woodcut (W.1376): a candidate derivation that has never been tested. The reference usually given is Galster 53: Galster 1936, p. 40, covers the medals per Mortensen's citation, but whether no. 53 spans both variants is unverified, and Friis sources the two variants to two different national corpora — a Danish corpus for the smaller, the 1852 Bohemian-medals catalogue alone for the larger. Specimens are recorded in the Royal Collection of Coins and Medals in Copenhagen (Beckett saw two there, one silver and one bronze, with slightly different portraits), and Friis placed the fine larger specimen — probably silver, gilt, apparently chased — in the k.k. Mønt- og Medaillesamling in Vienna; the 'one at Prague' of the older literature is a citation ghost, resting on a page of Friis that names only the Prague-published catalogue of 1852 describing the larger variant, not any Prague holding. And Mortensen's caution matters — what survives in public cabinets is, as a rule, aftercasts rather than original strikings, and a specimen sold at auction in 2022 was a cast gilt electrotype.

The engraving is reproduced here because no openly licensed photograph of a specimen has been located; Nationalmuseet did photograph the obverse of its own specimen for Tycho Brahes Verden (2006), fig. 3, printed p. 89 (PDF p. 87) — the caption confirms that specimen as the smaller, motto variant, and gives no inventory number.
images.nature: Two variants exist — a larger of c. 39 mm with the verse legend and a smaller of c. 35 mm with the motto. Whether specimens were STRUCK in Tycho's lifetime is a separate and softer question from whether the design is his: Friis says the Copenhagen piece 'synes at være støbt' — appears to be CAST from a pierced example — and Mortensen generalises that public cabinets hold these medals 'i Reglen kun i Afstøbninger', usually only as casts. Against this stands a counter-witness: the Danske Magazin compilers of 1746 state that they personally inspected two 'Originaler' — one silver in the Royal Coin Cabinet, one base-metal in Klevenfeldt's collection — and describe specimens as 'afstemplede', struck. That is a live, unresolved conflict between primary accounts 125 years apart. The Nationalmuseet-photographed specimen (the smaller variant) shows no visible piercing at the rim.

images.label: The aetatis-50 portrait (Skokloster / Edinburgh) — the exile likeness

bounds.argument: The dating rests on two different texts, not one. The surviving Skokloster and Edinburgh canvases carry a third-person caption — 'ÆTATIS SVÆ ANNO 50 COMPLETO … QVO POST DIVTINVM IN PATRIA EXILIVM LIBERTATI DESIDERATÆ DIVINO PROVISV RESTITVTVS EST' — with no place and no year, verified by direct examination of high-resolution photographs of both canvases and by SHM's own catalogue transcription. The dated text is attested only on the lost Copenhagen picture, via Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses (1668), pp. 335–336: first person ('restitutus fui'), placed and dated VANDESBECHI AN. MDXCVII, and signed TYCHO BRAHE OT. That exemplar's year is settled at 1597 — Resen's apostrophus numeral; Dreyer 1890, p. 264, verified against the printed page image; TBOO IX.211, sourced in its own apparatus to Cod. Vindob. lat. 10686; DSL's '1598' is a transcription slip in the modern digital edition. The lower bound of 14 December 1596, the day Tycho completed his fiftieth year, follows from 'aetatis suae anno 50 completo' and stands; but the 1597 anchor transfers to the surviving canvases by type-identity inference only, since their own captions are undated.

images.description: The last new likeness type made in Tycho's lifetime, and the one that shows him as he left Denmark: half-length, bareheaded and balding at fifty, in a black gold-buttoned doublet with an immense lace-edged ruff, a broad ornamented gold belt, rings on both hands and a pair of gloves held in the left. Two gold chains carry the enamelled Order of the Elephant on his breast. In the upper left corner an emblem panel shows a cone with a ball finial on a stepped pedestal, under a draped canopy suspended by cords from a hand emerging from cloud, flanked by winged putti; on the Skokloster canvas its inscribed band reads STANS TEGOR IN SOLIDO VENT[·] STREPAT IGNIS ET VNDA. The gold inscription fills the upper right. It is independent of the 1586 Gemperlin likeness family — a fresh sitting, from a man a decade older than the face the engravings kept reprinting. Versions are at Skokloster Castle in Sweden (the one shown here) and at the Royal Observatory Edinburgh in the Crawford collection, with a further version in the Nationalmuseum-administered portrait collection at Gripsholm Castle (NMGrh 1580). The leading account of the sitting is production in the Wandsbek exile itself, in 1597 — the place and year named by the dated inscription of the lost Copenhagen exemplar; the two painter entries in Tycho's own diary — the unexplained painter working on Hven from 6 March to 23 April 1591, and the 'Pictor' of 4 May 1596 — remain as residual alternatives for an earlier underlying likeness.
images.image_credit: Portrait of Tycho Brahe, aetatis 50 (1596–97), oil on canvas. Skoklosters slott, Sweden, inv. 11593_SKO. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons — high-resolution surrogate: Commons 'Porträtt av Tycho Brahe - Skoklosters slott - 90153.tif' (3253 × 4007 px, Skoklosters Slott/SHM), from which the emblem band was read (STANS TEGOR IN SOLIDO VENT[·] STREPAT IGNIS ET VNDA). The support is given as canvas by the holding institution and by Mortensen 1946; the 2006 Nationalmuseet catalogue calls it oil on wood, and that conflict is unresolved.
images.nature: Original LOST. Every located painting of this type is a copy, and the best of them are copies of a lost picture rather than of one another. Ståhlbrand 1946 (p.133): of contemporary painted portraits made in Tycho's lifetime 'quite certainly none are preserved to our day'; and (p.134) 'the original is quite certainly destroyed, but several replicas exist. The best copy is the one at Skokloster.' Håkansson (ed.) 2006, p.133, agrees that the Skokloster canvas is 'probably a copy of a contemporary painting that has been lost'. Mortensen 1946 catalogues seven paintings of the type and calls every one of them a copy.

images.label: The painted portraits in the finest Mechanica copies — Tycho between Ptolemy and Copernicus

bounds.argument: The Mechanica was produced from January 1598, which sets the campaign's lower bound; Tycho's death on 24 October 1601 caps it, and the bulk of the presentation copies had gone out by about 1600. The Copenhagen copy's autograph dedication of 18 September 1600 is that exemplar's terminus ante quem. The former lower-bound basis — an 'Aet: LII' age inscription on the watercolours — is withdrawn: full-resolution inspection of the Copenhagen leaf (July 2026) found no age inscription of any kind, Mortensen's actual printed reading is 'Aet: LI', type-generic and anchored to Andersen's 1886 etching rather than to any leaf, and Vellev's 'LII' remains unlocated.

images.description: The grandest copies of the Mechanica (Wandsbek 1598) carry, on the leaf facing the title, a hand-painted watercolour portrait made individually for that copy — for the three dedicated exemplars (Copenhagen, Strahov, Weimar) demonstrably the last portrait campaign of Tycho's life, and the only one where each impression is unique; for the undedicated pair (Stockholm KVA and Kalocsa), which carry neither dedicatee nor dispatch date, a post-1601 completion by the heirs or Tengnagel cannot be formally excluded, though no post-death dispatch of any Mechanica copy is documented. The composition is a claim as much as a likeness. The bust sits in a blue oval; two winged putti above hold a cartouche lettered 'Effigies Tychonis Brahe'; below, two bearded figures in gold, lettered on their plinths COPERNICVS (left) and PTOLOMEVS (right), each lean on a gilt armillary sphere and gesture toward the arms roundel between them, around which runs Tycho's motto 'Esse potius quam haberi' — the astronomer placing himself, literally, between the two authorities his own system was built to supersede. He wears a fur-lined black gown over a gold brocade doublet with a heavy linked chain, a black belt, and holds a small dark object in his left hand. Despite Friis's and Mortensen's readings of an Elephant device on the chain, the full-resolution image shows no figurative pendant — the chain ends in a plain knot. Four exemplars are recorded by Mortensen: the Royal Library in Copenhagen, the Royal Library in Stockholm, the Strahov monastery in Prague, and the cathedral library at Kalocsa in Hungary. The Copenhagen exemplar is identified here as Det Kongelige Bibliotek, LN 432 2°, eks. 2 — Tycho's own presentation copy to Petr Vok z Rožmberka (Peter Wok von Rosenberg), lord of Krumlov and Třeboň, which carries in one volume its silk presentation binding stamped with Tycho's gilt portrait supralibros, Rožmberk's engraved ex-libris of 1609, Tycho's autograph dedication ('Dono Dat', signed Tycho Brahe and dated 'Anno 1600 Septembris Die 18'), and the watercolour on the leaf facing the title. Nationalmuseet reproduced this leaf in Tycho Brahes Verden (2006), fig. 8, credited to the Royal Library.
images.image_credit: The hand-painted watercolour portrait facing the title of Tycho Brahe, Astronomiæ instauratæ mechanica (Wandsbek 1598). From KB's own digitisation, Digitale Samlinger object11914, leaf LN_432_2_005 (IIIF: kb-images.kb.dk/DAMJP2/online_master_arkiv_4/non-archival/HA/TB_LN432/).

The Mechanica census's watercolour subgroup (event E042) currently lists only Weimar, KVA and Kalocsa; it should include both copenhagen-kb-ln-432-copy3 and prague-strahov-h23-hasenburg.
images.nature: Each watercolour is unique — hand-painted individually for its copy, so every one is an original, and no two are quite alike. Vellev's claim that they 'must all derive from the same model' is refuted for at least one leaf: a first-hand inspection of the Weimar leaf found it a replica of the de Gheyn 1590 engraving, captioned aetatis 40 / anno 1586 — a demonstrably different and much earlier model.

Majestatis a Consiliis, Domino et amico suo in primis honorando Tycho Brahe'. Von Biela's letter was published in Astronomische Nachrichten III (1825), p. 256. He describes the Copenhagen copy first — 'I det store kongelige Bibliothek i Kjøbenhavn findes et Exemplar af Bogen, i hvilket der paa Bagsiden af Titelbladet er anbragt et med Vandfarve malet Portræt' — and then: 'I dette Exemplar af Bogen findes en af Tyge Brahe selv underskreven Dedikation til den bøhmiske Adelsmand Peter Vok von Rosenberg.' He then turns to 'et andet Exemplar … i Præmonstratenserklostret Strahof i Prag', whose autograph dedication is to Johann Liber Baro ab Hasenburg. Studnička 1901 (pp. 44–48) independently gives the Strahov copy as a presentation copy to Baron Johann von Hasenburg, in an accompanying autograph letter, in a green silk binding with the portrait supralibros on the front and the arms on the back.
