images.label: The Týn church epitaph, Prague — the effigy that closes the series

bounds.lower: 1604 (Kirstine's death — the only sourced terminus post quem for the erection; the 1601 burial dates the grave, not the monument)
bounds.argument: Tycho died in Prague on 24 October 1601 and was buried in the Týn church, but the monument's erection is sourced only as after his widow Kirstine's death in 1604 (Friis 1871 p. 298, Mortensen 1946 p. 74, Norlind 1970 p. 318); no source attests an earlier figure-stone phase. It therefore stands past the lifetime boundary — but it was made in Prague by people who had seen him, and it closes the series.

images.description: The memorial relief in the Church of Our Lady before Týn: Tycho carved life-size in red Slivenec marble, 200 × 115 cm, standing in a suit of armour already old-fashioned in his own day, his right hand resting on a globe set upon the family arms and his left on his sword hilt, a plumed helmet at his feet. The prosthetic nose is plainly shown. The carving is coarse, and the workshop is unattributed — Mortensen (1946, without citation) called it Austrian, by type-resemblance to the Berka von Dauba monument in the same church (a comparandum itself unverified); Vellev (2006, equally uncited) takes it for a local Prague stonemason's workshop responsible for a series of monuments in Prague churches. It was ground down and restored for the tercentenary in 1901, when the floor slab lettered simply TYCHO BRAHE was also laid. Casts are at Frederiksborg (inv. A 155, maker 'Steffensen', 1885–86) and in the Round Tower's historical collection in Copenhagen (a life-size plaster made c. 1867 from the original by F. R. Friis, transferred from the Nationalmuseet) — both pre-dating the 1901 restoration. It is the last image of Tycho made from living memory, and the point where the lifetime iconography hands over to the printed afterlife.
images.image_credit: The memorial relief in the Church of Our Lady before Týn, Prague. Photograph by Arpasevan, released CC0 via Wikimedia Commons.
images.nature: An original carved monument, made in Prague by people who had seen him — but set up after his death, and heavily restored in 1901.

whereabouts.summary: In situ in the Church of Our Lady before Týn, Prague, against a pier near the chancel.
whereabouts.tier: located (architecturally fixed; the 2010 reinterment campaign necessarily handled it)
whereabouts.note: Red Slivenec marble, 200 × 115 cm (Mortensen 1942 gives 2.03 × 1.15 m). Figure-stone and inscription plate are physically distinct elements (Vellev 2006), but no source dates them separately: Friis 1871 and Norlind 1970 describe a single erection by the heirs after Kirstine's death in 1604, and a two-campaign history is this project's hypothesis, unattested. The epitaph text was composed by Jakob Typotius. The death year was miscut MDCIII for MDCI and patched with coloured filler (Vellev 2006, p. 230); the upper plate gives 29 October against the frame's XXIV OCTOB (Vellev 2006, p. 232). Four-ancestor arms Brahe/Bille/Rud/Ulfstand, with only two helmets where four belong (Vellev 2006, p. 230) — on Vellev's explanation possibly deliberate economy, since all four families sometimes used the same buffalo-horn-and-peacock-feather crest. Restored in 1901 by Jan Herain for the tercentenary: surfaces cleaned and smoothed, the ground painted white, cornices repaired, letters blackened, and the missing top ornament replaced by a small obelisk; Herain's measurements and notes of the work were no longer to be found as of 2006 (Vellev p. 235). Of the two Copenhagen casts, the identification of Frederiksborg A 155 as the Týn figure is well-supported inference — structured record, catalogue photograph, independent 1937 corroboration — not a documentary source naming both together.

conflicts.question: Is the globe terrestrial or celestial?
conflicts.positions: Celestial — Studnička 1901 ('Himmelsglobus', primary autopsy, German original verified); the Czech descriptions ('nebeská sféra') are unverified. Terrestrial — Vellev's Danish text in the 2006 volume ('symbolsk jordglobus', p. 230). The 2006 English summary (p. 275; printed 277) says only 'a globe', unqualified — it is not a witness to either side.
conflicts.status: open: one verified witness each way (Studnička 1901 celestial; Vellev 2006 Danish text terrestrial); the 2006 English summary is neutral, so the volume does not contradict itself; no surrogate — including the 1894 pre-restoration engraving — shows surface markings on the globe; and Herain's 1901 grinding means the present surface cannot arbitrate the original

versions.support: copper engraving, printed on the text page
versions.verdict: the earliest printed record of the monument, and the witness to its pre-1901 state
versions.note: Attributed to Johann Martin Bernigeroth by the 2006 volume; the plate as printed carries no engraver's signature legible at 600 dpi and the 1746 text names none, so do not harden the attribution. The 1746 text documents the production chain: drawn in 1743 in Prague for Tycho de Hofman, the Danish Chancery secretary there for Maria Theresa's Bohemian coronation, and engraved for his Portraits historiques (The Hague, 1746), the plate then lent to Danske Magazin (bind 2, pp. 356–57) — naming the commissioner but no engraver. The Bernigeroth attribution traces to Vellev's fig.-3 caption alone, and his 'efter Danske Magazin' could even describe a later derivative. A collation trap: it is printed on the text page at the head of p. 353, not on an inserted leaf.
versions.source: Grinder-Hansen ed. 2006, fig. 3; autopsy of the 1746 volume

images.label: The Brahe coat-of-arms supralibros
images.description: Tycho's armorial stamp, impressed in gold as the lower-board partner of the portrait oval: on every binding in the attested corpus where both boards have actually been examined — presentation copies and own-library bindings alike — the two ovals travel together as a matched die-pair (Kleinschnitzová states outright that Tycho used the pair on both classes; Prandtl's 1932 frontispiece shows the UT Austin Gesner with gilt ovals on both boards; Mosley photographs both covers of a presentation Epistolae). The device is the plain undifferenced Brahe paternal shield — sable, a pale argent — under helm, coronet and a tall panache crest, not an ancestral marshalling (Grinder-Hansen; Vellev). It is ringed by a motto in an oval medallion ('Arma, genus, fundi pereunt, durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent' — 'arms, lineage, estates perish; virtue and learning hold nobility's lasting honour'); per Dreyer's apparatus in TBOO IX, 175, the couplet was printed by Tycho's own press at Uraniborg in 1584 — some four years before the die's earliest dated impression — so the stamp adopted an existing text, and the same distich recurs on the reverse of the larger (39 mm) 1595 medal. The familiar claim that the arms occur 'in the same two sizes as the portrait stamp' rests on Mortensen's single joint clause for portrait-and-arms together (7.6 × 5.8 / 5.8–5.9 × 4.3 cm, internally inconsistent between his 1931 and 1966 articles); he never measured the arms oval separately, and the first independent measurement — the Stockholm KB De mundi, ≈6.6 × 5.3 cm from the KB scan on a transferred scale — fits neither figure.
images.census_copies: ARMS supralibros documented on: Stockholm KB De mundi RAR: 106 A (arms on the lower cover, verified first-hand from the KB scan, p. 493); Görlitz De mundi (dedication copy to Bartholomäus Scultetus, 8 May 1588, per Norlind p. 127 — the earliest dated arms attestation); Smithsonian/Dibner Epistolae (arms supralibros on covers). The Wolfenbüttel Epistolae HAB Astronomica 8 line (arms + motto on back cover, behind the portrait front) is unreconciled — the 2026-07-15 sweep logged Wolfenbüttel as a null vector; a direct HAB query is pending. The Bodleian Savile De mundi is a documented negative (no supralibros on either cover).
images.image_credit: The gilt arms supralibros, stamped in gold on the lower cover of a parchment binding; the photographed copy has not been identified.
images.nature: An original stamp, surviving only as impressions; the die is untraced, as with the portrait die.

whereabouts.summary: Impressions survive on the back covers of Tycho's presentation and library bindings.
whereabouts.holder: Documented on the Strahov Mechanica (arms on the back, portrait on the front of the same volume)
whereabouts.tier: extant as impressions; the die untraced
whereabouts.note: Also on Wolfenbüttel HAB Astronomica 8 and the Smithsonian/Dibner Epistolae.

conflicts.question: Was the front/back split really portrait-for-gifts, arms-for-library?
conflicts.positions: The 2006 book's own caption says the PORTRAIT die was used on 'gaveeksemplarer af sine egne bøger samt nogle af bindene i hans eget bibliotek' — gift copies AND some bindings in his own library. Kleinschnitzová 1933 records six own-library Clementinum volumes with the ovals, and Strahov Σ V 5 is a Tycho supralibros on a book he did not write.
conflicts.status: settled: the split is affirmatively contradicted — the ovals travel as a pair on both presentation and own-library bindings (Kleinschnitzová explicit; zero single-oval bindings in the ~25–30 examined objects; the unchecked interiors — GKS 306, Kalocsa, Grimani, Sign. 14 G 30 — declared as missing data)

images.label: The inserted author portrait in Epistolae and Mechanica copies
images.description: The engraved portrait was inserted loose — often hand-coloured — in copies of the Epistolae (1596) and in presentation copies of the Mechanica (1598): the interior complement to the gilt portrait on the cover. For the Epistolae, printed at Uraniborg, the cause is documented — Tycho's press had no intaglio capability. The Mechanica was printed at Wandsbek by Philipp von Ohr, a printer styled Chalcographus, whose shop supplied four integral copperplates for that very book; there the operative constraint was custody of the de Gheyn plate, not the absence of a press. Practice varied copy by copy — engraved impressions, watercolour substitutes, and copies with no portrait at all are documented. The Smithsonian/Dibner Epistolae carries a hand-coloured impression of the second engraving, identified by direct examination (2026).
images.image_credit: The de Gheyn engraved portrait, of the kind inserted — often hand-coloured — in copies of the Epistolae and the Mechanica. Statens Museum for Kunst, Den Kongelige Kobberstiksamling, Copenhagen, inv. KKSgb7084. Public Domain Mark.
images.nature: Original engraved impressions, inserted loose — often hand-coloured: at Uraniborg (Epistolae, 1596) because the press had no intaglio capability; at Wandsbek (Mechanica, 1598) despite the printer's copperplate capacity — the constraint there was custody of the de Gheyn plate.

whereabouts.summary: Copy-level: engraved impression, watercolour substitute, or no portrait at all — what a given volume carries varies precisely because insertion was loose.
whereabouts.tier: extant as impressions inside surviving copies
whereabouts.note: The Smithsonian/Dibner Epistolae impression was identified as the second engraving (v2) by marker examination of the full-resolution digitisation (this project, 2026-07-18); no institutional catalogue states the plate, and the insertion date into that volume is undetermined (earliest documented owner: Uffenbach).

images.label: The small gilt brass quadrant — an iconographic instrument
images.description: A small gilt brass quadrant carrying a deliberate iconographic programme — Nonnian subdivisions (Pedro Nunes's nested-arc method of graduation, which Tycho himself found insufficient in practice) and 'an emblem of life and death' — rather than serving only as a measuring tool; a point where the Instruments and Iconography pillars meet, the instrument as image. Built c. 1573 in Denmark: Thoren (Lord of Uraniborg, p.75 n.5) anchors the date on Tycho's own log of the lunar eclipse of 8 December 1573 (TBOO X, 38–39), which he reports contains an unambiguous reference to this instrument. Christianson's caption (On Tycho's Island, p.257, Fig.51) — 'probably built c.1568–69 with Hugo Blotius in Basel' — does depict this very instrument, but the date carries no citation, contradicts his own adjoining prose, and is dropped in his 2020 Measure of the Heavens; it is retained here as recorded dissent. The quadrant opens the Mechanica (1598) on an engraved (intaglio) plate, where most of the book's images are woodcuts. Its motto reads VIVIMVS INGENIO, CÆTERA MORTIS ERVNT — first-person plural, against the impersonal 'Vivitur ingenio' of the adage tradition — and the emblem's description is independently attested in the 1591 instrument synopsis for Landgrave Wilhelm IV (TBOO VI, 284–285, item XXV) and in Resen 1668 (pp.344–345, the same emblem executed on the Stjerneborg wall); these witnesses fix the description by 1591 but do not date the instrument's construction. The subject of a dedicated iconographic study (Perkins & Taub 2015, now read in full); the one earlier study, Segonds 1994, is cited but remains unread.
images.nature: The instrument is DESTROYED, and the emblem it carried is NOT a portrait of Tycho. Tycho's own description (Opera Omnia V, p.14) calls the figure 'Juvenis laurea insignitus' — a laurel-crowned young man holding a celestial globe and a book. Neither Tycho, nor Perkins & Taub 2015, nor the 2006 book identifies him as Tycho. The record is kept because the emblem belongs to Tycho's self-presentation programme, not because it depicts him.

whereabouts.summary: Untraced after the Hven era. The Prague-destruction account is collective (Dreyer, hedged) and item-level documentation is absent from the 1607–1650 Prague inventories; the instrument was obsolete by c.1580 and its presence in the 1600 Prague shipment is unconfirmed.
whereabouts.tier: untraced
whereabouts.note: Dreyer 1890 pp.365–66: 'At the present day there is neither at Prague nor at Copenhagen the smallest vestige of Tycho's celebrated instruments' — his own hedge 'are said to have' on the 1619 destruction is preserved. Only the great brass globe survived, and it burned at Copenhagen in October 1728. The Detmold Mechanica (Lippische Landesbibliothek Nl 70.4°) is the only public deep-zoom surrogate of the plate (IIIF manifest digitale-sammlungen.llb-detmold.de/i3f/v20/2547750/manifest, plate at canvas 2547769), but its emblem roundel is uncoloured line-work within an otherwise richly hand-coloured plate; the red/green emblem colouring is known only from BL C.45.h.3 (Perkins & Taub Fig. 3), which has no digital surrogate.

conflicts.question: Date of the instrument
conflicts.positions: c. 1573 — Perkins & Taub 2015 p.11. Built c. 1568–69 with Blotius in Basel — Christianson. 1569 Augsburg — this catalogue, 2026-05-07.
conflicts.status: resolved in favour of c.1573 (Thoren, Dec 1573 eclipse log); Christianson's 1568–69 retained as recorded uncited dissent; '1569 Augsburg' marked as a house conflation with the great Augsburg quadrant, corrected 2026-07-18

conflicts.question: What the emblem shows
conflicts.positions: 'An astronomer with an ASTROLABE' ('en astronom med et astrolabium') — Birgitte Bøggild Johannsen, in essay prose (not a caption) at Grinder-Hansen ed. 2006, p.219; her Danish rendering of the motto is nonetheless first-person plural, incidentally corroborating VIVIMVS. 'One hand holds a CELESTIAL GLOBE, the other a BOOK' — Tycho, Opera Omnia V p.14.
conflicts.status: the 2006 book is wrong; there is no astrolabe in the emblem

images.label: The printed views of Uraniborg and Stjerneborg
images.description: Tycho controlled the image of his establishment as carefully as his own likeness. The earliest graphic representation is the Orthographia broadsheet — three woodcuts of Uraniborg in elevation, bird's-eye view and ground-plan, printed by early 1585 on Nielsen's own hedged inference — one print with several attested distributions (to Rantzau in 1585, to Wilhelm IV in 1586, to Blotius in 1592), surviving in the exemplar sent on 1 March 1586 to Wilhelm IV (Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, Best. 3 II, Nr. 1070) and retrieved on loan by Eiler Nystrom in 1912. How the Uraniborg view in Braun & Hogenberg's Civitates orbis terrarum descends from it is a point on which the two 1921 authorities disagree: Nielsen (Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen) holds the Braun plate a direct copy of the Marburg sheet, while Beckett & Christensen derive it from the lost 1585 woodcut sent to Hajek, the Vienna pen-drawing being a collateral witness and explicitly not the direct model. The Braun & Hogenberg plate (engraved Cologne 1586; published 1588 in the atlas's fourth volume) added a map of Hven and the 'Apotheosis of the Sound' (Christianson, figs. 21–22). The Mechanica (1598) carries the celebrated plates of Uraniborg, Stjerneborg and their instruments, but adds only one new architectural image — the east facade, a copperplate — and otherwise reprints the 1596 Epistolae blocks, so that 1598 dates the printing, not the image, for the reused views. Through these printed views the long-demolished buildings are still known. Beckett & Christensen's 1921 study established the reliability of the sequence: the Marburg broadsheet is the most reliable, carrying details found nowhere else; the Epistolae (1596) and Mechanica (1598) views are progressively prettified but less accurate; and the Epistolae map of Hven derives from a drawing by Willem Blaeu, Tycho's pupil. Measured against Charlier's 1901 excavation, all of them are unreliable in architectural detail — corrected by Charles Christensen's measured reconstruction (see Loca).
images.image_credit: Orthographia praecipuae domus arcis Uraniburgi — the hand-coloured elevation and ground plan of Uraniborg, from Tycho Brahe, Astronomiae Instauratae Mechanica (Wandsbek, 1598). Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Copenhagen (Nielsen 432). Public domain.
images.nature: Original printed views, controlled by Tycho as carefully as his own likeness. Edition multiples.

whereabouts.summary: Survive wherever the books survive; the plate reproduced here is from the Royal Danish Library's copy.
whereabouts.tier: located (KB's digitised hand-coloured exemplar)

conflicts.question: Engraving or woodcut?
conflicts.positions: Christianson: the Mechanica has '22 woodcuts and engravings of Tycho's instruments, a new ENGRAVING of Uraniborg, and WOODCUTS of Hven, Stjerneborg and Tycho's imprese'. A collation of the 1602 reissue lists the Stjerneborg plans among nineteen full-page WOODCUTS, with only six copperplates in the whole book.
conflicts.status: The east-facade view is a new copperplate (Beckett's 'Kobberstikkeren', p. 10); the Stjerneborg views are woodcuts; the instrument plates are MIXED woodcut and engraving (Nielsen's collation of entry 432 tags the volume 'Træsn. og Kobberstik'; Horáček 2021 names three new 1598 instrument engravings). Open tension: Beckett assigns the fol. 84 ground-plan to the reused woodblocks, but its line quality in the KB scan matches the engraved facade — possibly design reused, block re-engraved

conflicts.question: Date of the Stjerneborg views
conflicts.positions: Beckett & Christensen 1921 p. 25 (PDF p. 29) record that the two Stjerneborg woodcuts had already appeared in the Epistolae (1596), and that the Mechanica repeats ('gentagne') the same two woodcuts. (The previously cited p. 41 is the unrelated van Paschen/Stenwinkel architects passage.)
conflicts.status: Beckett's block-reuse claim is now page-verified Tier-1 ('Klodserne … benyttede', p. 10; 'gentagne', p. 25) and extends to the Hven map, bird's-eye and ground-plan: 1598 dates the printing, not the image, for all but the east facade. The pixel-level defect-match remains undone — no true 1596 Epistolae digitisation was locatable (e-rara Rar 4403 is the 1601 Hulsius reissue; the census-confirmed 1596 Wolfenbüttel copy has no surrogate URL)

conflicts.question: The L+B monogram on the Epistolae east-facade view
conflicts.positions: The Epistolae (1596) east-facade woodcut (Beckett's Fig. 12) carries a monogram of the letters L and B on a pillar left of the gallery. Beckett (1921, p. 8 with its endnote) reads the year as presumably 1590 — his own hedge; Friis (Bidrag til dansk Kunsthistorie, p. 4) read the numerals as (15)96 and, in Beckett's view, misreproduced the monogram.
conflicts.status: undecided on present evidence; the cutter is unidentified — Nagler and Hollstein were not checked this run (a tool failure, not a researched negative), and Lambert Cornelisz does not fit on initials or floruit

images.label: The posthumous copies (1602 onward)
images.description: After Tycho's death (October 1601) his engineered image kept propagating from the de Gheyn plates. The Nuremberg branch runs through two plates one generation apart: an unsigned same-direction copy of the second engraving, cut for Hülsius's press for the 1601 Epistolarum, and the 1602 Mechanica plate cut in turn from that copy — the two share the same idiosyncratic caption errors, with identical line-breaks. The first plate itself, in Prague by 1602, printed integrally in at least one examined Progymnasmata copy (Copenhagen), though two further copies examined at full resolution carry no portrait at all — a small or copy-specific press-run rather than the edition's norm. Impressions lettered 'Marco Sadeler excudit' are restrikes from the original copper, though the date of that address and the identity of the Sadeler behind it are unresolved. Jacob van Meurs re-cut the type half a century on for the 1655 Hague edition of Gassendi's biography. So far as traced, the century's engraved portrait copies descend from the two Amsterdam plates; the exceptions are the Rudolphine Tables frontispiece figure of 1627, engraved by Georg Celer (Cöler) of Nuremberg in a distinct engraved lineage whose ultimate model is undetermined, and two unattributed woodcuts whose models are likewise undetermined.
images.nature: The copy-stemma of the two engraved Amsterdam plates only; carved, painted, and instrument-borne likenesses are treated in their own records (icon-blaeu-globes, icon-console-clock-1642, icon-teyn-epitaph, icon-standing-type).

whereabouts.summary: Dispersed edition multiples across European collections.
whereabouts.tier: extant as impressions and objects
whereabouts.note: The Nuremberg descent runs through two plates one generation apart: the unsigned copy-plate cut for Hülsius's press for the 1601 Epistolarum, and the 1602 Mechanica plate cut from it, repeating its caption errors with identical line-breaks.

conflicts.question: Does EVERY seventeenth-century image descend from the two Amsterdam plates?
conflicts.positions: The engraved gilt-brass side plate of a 1642 console clock (Nationalmuseet, inv. D138 — a number itself unverified: one direct fetch of the museum portal finds the object but no date, a portal search returns null, and the number is absent from the 2006 book's p. 146) shows Tycho pointing at his own world system, and the 2006 book identifies its model as the copperplate in Kepler's Rudolphine Tables (1627) — a frontispiece engraved by Georg Celer (Cöler) of Nuremberg (Gattei p. 363; the engraver's sheet is GNM Nuremberg, inv. MP 2799). Whether the clock's face (as opposed to its pose) is de Gheyn-derived remains open on the borrowed-head/invented-body pattern; object-level detail is treated at icon-console-clock-1642.
conflicts.status: the universal claim was too strong as written. The Rudolphine lineage shows Tycho as proprietor of a world system rather than as a face; whether it is fully independent of de Gheyn or carries a de Gheyn-derived face on an invented body is undetermined — no visual collation exists either way

open_questions: Per-copy portrait survey: the four Copenhagen (KB) Progymnasmata copies, the 1603/1610 issue-states, and surviving 1601 and 1610 Epistolarum witnesses — decisive for the titelauflage soft point (whether the 1610 reissue could have required a fresh portrait pull).
Digitaler Portraitindex records 41–91 remain unexamined (stateful pagination defeats non-interactive fetching); needs an interactive browser session — the counterexample sweep is not closed.
Thieme-Becker Band XXIX Sadeler entry (pp. 299–303) unopened — the one standard authority on the Sadelers not yet consulted.
Date of the 'Marco Sadeler excudit' address on New Hollstein 238 State II — New Hollstein gives none.
Portrait-leaf mechanics of the Epistolarum issues (integral title-verso versus inserted plate leaf) — decides how absolute the titelauflage reading of the 1610 reissue is.
Models of the two unattributed LWL Münster woodcuts and of the Freher 1688 Theatrum book-portrait — undetermined.

Whether the 1654 Paris first printing of Gassendi's Vita carries any portrait — the van Meurs plate is documented only in Vlacq's Hague 1655 second edition, and this record's 1655 end-date and icon-gassendi-frontispiece must agree on that basis.

images.label: The Gassendi Vita frontispiece (1655) — the portrait's afterlife
images.maker: Jacob van Meurs I (Amsterdam, c. 1619/20 – 1679), after Jacques de Gheyn II. The signature 'I.v.Meurs. Scul.' appears only in the state used in 1655; the 1654 state is unsigned, so the cutting — complete by 1654 — is attributed to van Meurs from the same-plate identity, while his signing of the 1655 state is documented.
images.description: The engraved Tycho portrait of Gassendi's Tychonis Brahei Vita — bound before Book One of the 1654 Paris first edition, and moved to the frontispiece slot in the 1655 Hague edition: a bust of Tycho in a flat turned-down collar and a single doubled chain, without the Frederik II medal, within a triumphal arch hung with his sixteen ancestral coats-of-arms, captioned 'Effigies Tychonis Brahe Ottonidis Dani… ætatis suæ anno 40, anno Dni 1586', with his motto 'Non Haberi sed Esse' ('not to seem, but to be') in the lower corners. It copies de Gheyn's second engraving — established not by the caption or the sixteen quarterings, which are identical in both de Gheyn states, but by the dispositive discriminators: the tablet's HVENNA and INSTRVMENTORVMQVE ASTRONOMICORVM, the second state's RØNNOR and STORMVASE armorials, the plumed beret worn on the head, and the arms transposed as in the second state. It shows how Tycho's carefully self-fashioned image was reused, a half-century after his death, to authorise the first full biography.
images.image_credit: Jacob van Meurs I after Jacques de Gheyn II, engraved portrait of Tycho (New Hollstein 239 copy b), used in Gassendi's Tychonis Brahei Vita (Paris 1654; The Hague 1655). Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, RP-P-OB-23.512 — the signed state. CC0.
images.nature: A posthumous engraved copy after de Gheyn's second engraving (New Hollstein 239 copy b): in use unsigned before Book One of the 1654 Paris first edition, then signed by Jacob van Meurs I ('I.v.Meurs. Scul.') as frontispiece of the 1655 Hague edition.

whereabouts.summary: An edition multiple: found in copies of both the 1654 Paris first edition (unsigned, before Book One) and the 1655 Hague edition (signed, as frontispiece); no copy lacking it is documented, but no multi-copy collation has been made.
whereabouts.tier: extant as impressions
whereabouts.note: Pierre Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei … Vita, 2nd ed. (The Hague: Vlacq, 1655).

images.label: The Kågeröd epitaph, 1613 — Tycho kneeling among his parents' children
images.maker: Unrecorded; the Tycho head repainted between 1862 and c. 1895 — by Magnus Petersen according to Mortensen 1946 (unfootnoted and uncorroborated; Petersen is documented at the epitaph only as recorder of its pre-restoration state, Nationalmuseet inv. 572 / DMR-193014, 1860).

bounds.argument: The tablet is dated by its own erection, twelve years after Tycho's death.

images.description: The large painted epitaph to Otte Brahe and Beate Bille in Kågeröd church, showing the parents with their ten children kneeling under the Crucifixion: five sons from the father (Tyge, Steen, Knud, Axel, Jørgen) and five daughters from the mother (Lisbet, Maren, Margrethe, Kirsten, Sophie). The daughters kneel in strict birth order; the sons do not — Knud, the youngest, is placed third. Tycho is the figure nearest his father, identified by a painted gold label, 'Lerde Tyge B.' — the learned Tyge Brahe.
images.nature: An original 1613 panel — but NOT an independent likeness. The loss of the Tycho face is attested by Horace Marryat, visiting in 1860 ('of Tycho's scarcely a vestige remains', publ. 1862), whose plea for restoration also fixes the panel as still unrestored at publication; Mortensen 1946, who cites Marryat in the same footnote and is therefore not an independent second witness, reports the head completely flaked and repainted after the Frederiksborg portrait, attributing the repaint to Magnus Petersen — an attribution that is unfootnoted and uncorroborated (see maker). The repaint falls between 1862 (hard, from Marryat) and c. 1895 (probable, from the post-restoration reproduction Mortensen cites in Danmarks Adels Aarbog XII, itself unexamined); its model was necessarily a COPY of the Frederiksborg original, which burned 16–17 December 1859 — plausibly C. A. Jensen's 1838 copy, Mortensen's own surrogate for the type. The face is therefore a 19th-century derivative of the Gemperlin type sitting on a 1613 panel, and has no evidential value as a likeness.

whereabouts.summary: In situ in Kågeröds kyrka, Skåne. Placed in front of the blocked south portal (former vapenhus entrance) in the 1914 Wåhlin renovation; reportedly moved to the sacristy in the 2022 interior renovation (Regionmuseet Skåne KrM 2022:40 — title confirmed, report unread).
whereabouts.inv: Bebyggelseregistret anläggnings-ID 21300000008127 (church building; no object-level inventory number located; fastighet Svalöv Kågeröd 18:1)
whereabouts.tier: located (photographed in the church in 2021; handled during the 2020–22 restoration)
whereabouts.note: The 2006 book's credit line 'Nationalmuseet, Roberto Fortuna foto' is a PHOTOGRAPHIC credit only — the object is in Sweden and always has been. Note also that 'the fifth kneeling son' counts position from the left, the eldest son's place, not birth order.

open_questions: The full text of Regionmuseet Skåne KrM 2022:40 and the 2011 Skånes Målerikonservatorer condition assessment — the untested paint stratigraphy; until one is read, the reported total loss of the 1613 face has never been checked against physical evidence.

The Danmarks Adels Aarbog XII (1895) plate — whether it shows the repainted state, as Mortensen's characterisation implies but no one has verified, and whether it carries a draughtsman or restorer credit.
Nationalmuseet DMR-193014 at full resolution (6075 × 7415 px, never visually inspected) — and whether it is identical with the 'Tegning' Mortensen cites: its medium field reads 'photograph'.
Whether the gold label 'Lerde Tyge B.' is 1613 lettering or renewed.

images.label: Tycho's portrait on the celestial globes — a distribution channel begun in his lifetime
images.date: from 1594; Blaeu's Tychonic globes from 1597/98, portrait confirmed on extant specimens from 1603
images.maker: Jacob Floris van Langren and his sons Arnold (who cut the lettering) and Hendrik (the figures), per the globe's own imprint; then Willem Janszoon Blaeu (1571–1638).

bounds.upper: after 1630 (latest located specimen, Museo Galileo 348); terminal edition undetermined
bounds.argument: The practice begins with the van Langren globe of 1594 — the Tychonic (third) state of a 32.5-cm celestial line the family had issued since 1586 with pre-Tychonic positions (1586 Linköping; 1589 Greenwich GLB0099, positions probably Rudolf Snellius's; 1594 Frankfurt — Dekker, History of Cartography vol. 3, App. 6.1 nos. 130/137/148, verified verbatim 2026-08-04). Tycho's data and portrait were thus retrofitted onto an existing commercial product. Blaeu's own first celestial globe followed in 1597/98 (Dekker's census says 1597, Mosley p.246 says 1598, citing the same van der Krogt pages; Warner 1971, the arbiter, unread) — it survives only as 9 of 12 gores at Houghton Library, Harvard (*51-2459 PF), and whether the portrait zone is among them is indeterminate. Earliest extant Blaeu specimen with confirmed portrait presence remains 1603. At the upper end, the latest securely located portrait-bearing specimen is the Joan Blaeu globe of after 1630; no source names a terminal portrait-bearing edition.

images.description: A miniature engraved portrait of Tycho set into the printed gores of celestial globes — on the 1594 van Langren globe, a fully contemporary likeness with its own cartouche apparatus, read at object level in 2026 from Mosley's fig. 4.7: an age tablet ÆTATIS 47 (Tycho was 47 from 14 Dec 1593 to 13 Dec 1594 — the caption was computed fresh for the globe, where every de Gheyn print freezes age 40/1586), his motto NON HABERI SED ESSE compressed into one crowning tablet, BRAHER/BILLER banderoles in the print's own orthography, an Effigies tablet using Tycho's own foreign name for Hven ('in insula Scarlatina HVÆNA', an epithet whose only pre-1594 printed source is his own De mundi preface), a scroll counting ~800 stars from his observations plus ~200 southern stars from the ancients, and the privilege formula 'studio & consensu Nobilis Viri TYCHONIS BRAHE' — a composite not assemblable from a print alone, i.e. on-object evidence of a Tychonic information channel. The mechanism claim stays part documented, part inferred: Mosley's 'must have given' each maker a portrait impression remains his own uncited inference; what is documented is the sanction (the on-globe privilege citation, and Blaeu's six months at Uraniborg 1595–96). The miniature itself is a laterally reversed bust; a 2026 close read leans it toward the second de Gheyn design (beret worn, no Frederik II medal, single doubled chain, turned-down collar), which the corrected v2-design window (Feb–Mar 1592 to ≤5 Sept 1595) admits for 1594 — the earlier claim that it 'must descend from the 1590 engraving' rested on misreading v2's terminus ante quem as a post quem and is withdrawn; but an adversarial pass held the v2 reading at MEDIUM (a v1 reduced to a bust-in-oval, shedding parapet, medal and chains to miniaturization, is not excluded at halftone resolution — first-generation photography of the Frankfurt globe is the gate). The globes carried his face across Europe on somebody else's product, at no cost to him — and the convention propagated beyond any authorial supply: the Veen/Hondius globe of 1613 carries the portrait with the legend 'Effigies Nob. viri Tychonis Brahe... Aetatis 47' (Stevenson's transcription, verified) — the frozen age-47 pointing back to a 1593/94 model at a date when Tycho could not have furnished anything.
images.nature: Printed multiples on manufactured objects — originals of their kind. Not an afterlife phenomenon: the practice begins in Tycho's lifetime and at his own initiative.

whereabouts.summary: One van Langren globe of the 1594 Tychonic state survives (Frankfurt); the 32.5-cm van Langren celestial line survives in three copies across its states (1586 Linköping, 1589 Greenwich, 1594 Frankfurt), the earlier two pre-Tychonic and portrait-less. Of Blaeu globes of 1603: Oxford (inv. 23709, portrait museum-confirmed) and Rome (Biblioteca Angelica); the Science Museum London specimen (1980-1913) is the same edition but its record is portrait-silent — catalogue silence being demonstrably non-diagnostic (RMG's granular record of its own 1603 Blaeu, GLB0101, likewise omits the portrait that edition carries). Later states after 1621 and after 1630 (the Metropolitan Museum's, portrait unconfirmed though printed from the 1603 plates; the Accorsi-Ometto's, asserted in a caption; the Museo Galileo's, confirmed).
whereabouts.tier: located (record-level Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek entry: Historisches Museum Frankfurt, celestial globe, van Langren family, 1594, inv. X 14 609)
whereabouts.note: The sole survivor of the 1594 Tychonic state (Mosley pp.231–232, figs. 4.6/4.7) — the specimen that carries the record's lower bound. Provenance: the Frankfurt Ratsbibliothek, whose librarian Johann Martin Waldschmidt (from 1691) expanded the library into instruments; the museum's blog says presumably bought at the Frankfurt Book Fair (medium confidence; Glasemann 1999 pp.15–20, the museum's own catalogue, would settle it and is print-only). The latest securely located portrait-bearing specimen is the Joan Blaeu globe of after 1630 at the Museo Galileo, Florence, inv. 348 (diam. 680 mm, from the Medici collections; the catalogue notes 'There is a portrait of Tycho Brahe'). The Metropolitan Museum's Blaeu globe (1990.84, after 1621) is verified to exist and its 1990 acquisition bulletin states it prints from the 1603 plates — portrait presence therefore probable by plate identity but unobserved (both open-access photographs show the wrong hemispheres). The Oxford History of Science Museum's 1603 globe is inv. 23709, portrait confirmed by the museum. The 1613 portrait-bearing globe is RMG GLB0122 (535 mm), by Adriaen Veen with Jodocus Hondius Jr. On the Blaeu and Hondius-line globes the portrait sits in the southern hemisphere, below Cetus near Phoenix — the face museum photography systematically misses; on the 1594 van Langren globe it sits in the southern sky near Eridanus and Piscis Notius.

conflicts.question: Piety or marketing?
conflicts.positions: Grinder-Hansen 2006, p.245 (read at page level 2026-08-04): Blaeu 'producerede stjerneglober til det europæiske marked baseret på Tycho Brahes resultater — og pietetsfuldt forsynede med hans portræt' — 'pietetsfuldt' (piously) is his own word, though in that sentence he calls Blaeu only 'the Dutch cartographer who had been on Hven 1595–96', not a pupil. Mosley 2007 pp.248–249 documents the opposite mechanism at the origin — the image reached the makers in Tycho's lifetime with his sanction, 'to grant legitimacy to the instruments'.
conflicts.status: Mosley governs the origin — lifetime, sanctioned, privilege-documented; Grinder-Hansen's piety reading remains defensible for the posthumous continuation, which the record's own latest specimens embody, and the 1613 Veen/Hondius globe shows the convention self-propagating after 1601.

open_questions: First-generation photography of HMF X 14609 (write to the Historisches Museum Frankfurt): the single gate on the miniature's model (v2 design vs v1-reduced, held at MEDIUM), the unread right-hand cartouche, the States-General privilege term (ad decem read against Mosley's fifteen years), and pixel confirmation of ÆTATIS 47 on the object.

Whether the Houghton gore fragment of Blaeu's first celestial globe (9 of 12 gores, *51-2459 PF) includes the portrait zone — Warner, Imago Mundi 25 (1971) 29–38 is the arbiter (paywalled; on the Desiderata), and the call number itself has no live catalogue record (a reference query to Houghton would close both).

The Plancius–Hondius globe of 1597/98: Tier-2 sources put 'a portrait of Tycho below Cetus' in that globe's tradition, possibly by conflation with its 1602 Blaeu copy or the 1613 globe. Test object: the twelve gores found 1983 in the Nicolai Collection, Württembergische Landesbibliothek Stuttgart. If real, the lifetime portrait-globe census has two or three members, not one, and the 1613 Aetatis-47 legend may descend via the Hondius house.
The date of Blaeu's 10-cm celestial globe (Mosley: 'in the intervening period', with a Tycho attribution) — the one live remaining lifetime-globe candidate; van der Krogt 1993 pp. 503–505.
The month of the Hondius 1601 globe (Tycho died 24 Oct 1601) — its lifetime status is genuinely undetermined.

images.label: The 1642 console clock — Tycho as proprietor of a world system
images.maker: Unrecorded. The 2006 caption derives the Tycho figure from the Rudolphine Tables frontispiece (1627), without argument; the plates' Latin apparatus instead traces to Tycho's own publications (De mundi aetherei 1588; Epistolae astronomicae 1596), and a museum-affiliated inventory dates the object 1623, before the claimed model.

bounds.argument: The plates' Latin traces to Tycho's own prints (the 1588 De mundi heading recast third-person; the motto printed 1596); 1627 is a lower bound only if the caption's unverified pictorial derivation holds, and is impossible if the competing unfooted 1623 date (Frombork inventory) is right. 1642 rests on the unfootnoted 2006 caption; the museum record is undated and no engraved date or signature is visible in the 2006 photograph.

images.description: An engraved and gilt brass side plate from a console clock, paired with a matching Copernicus plate: the two astronomers stand pointing at their respective world systems. A banderole reads HYPOTYPOSIS Systematis mundani a Tychone inventi, with the motto 'Quid si sic'. A century after Copernicus, the Tychonic system still had its adherents, and this is what that looked like as a domestic object. The matching plate reads HYPOTYPOSIS Systematis mundi Copernicani, with the motto 'Sic movetur Mundus'.
images.nature: A posthumous derivative of contested lineage. Its Latin apparatus traces to Tycho's own publications (the 1588 De mundi heading recast in the third person; the Stjerneborg motto printed 1596); the 2006 caption's derivation from the Rudolphine frontispiece — where 'Quid si sic' also appears, as Kepler's plate quoting Tycho — is unargued, unverified for the figures (both stand here; the frontispiece's Copernicus sits), and impossible if the competing 1623 date is right. The paired-portrait scheme has a precedent in Tycho's own instrument decoration (Mechanica 1598). It remains the Iconographia's example of Tycho figured as proprietor of a cosmology rather than as a face.

whereabouts.summary: On display at the National Museum in Copenhagen, in the Renaissance galleries.
whereabouts.tier: located (record-level page on the museum's own database)
whereabouts.note: The museum's record carries NO object date — its 'Datering' field shows 1970–2014, which is photographic file metadata. The 1642 date rests on the 2006 caption alone. The museum's own image filename calls the plates 'Messing Døre', brass doors. Hinge-knuckle hardware and facing lock escutcheons visible in the 2006 photograph suggest the leaves are lockable doors, supporting the 'Messing Døre' filename against the catalogued 'sideplader'. The museum's image asset is persistently server-broken (HTTP 500, no Wayback copy), so the 2006 published photograph is the working surrogate. The Frombork instrument inventory dates the object 1623 without stated source.

images.label: Heinrich Hansen, 1882 — Tycho as national history painting
images.maker: Heinrich Hansen (1821–1890), architectural painter.

bounds.argument: Dated by the museum's catalogue record; corroborated by Eller 1978 (p. 43, 'Rekonstruktion af Heinrich Hansen 1882') and the 'H.H. 82' monogram reported on the sister version.

images.description: 'Uranienborg på Hveen': Anders Sørensen Vedel presents the first Danish collection of ballads to Queen Sophie in Tycho's presence. The museum's A 154, a nocturne of Stjerneborg, is by the same artist, from the same year, and hangs in the same room — Hven by day and by night — and both canvases sit within the museum's founding-era history-painting programme (J. C. Jacobsen's foundation, royal decree of 5 April 1878; the programme abandoned c. 1890, per Eller 1978); but no commission record has been recovered for either canvas, and no source uses pair or pendant language. By the 1880s Tycho had become a figure of national costume drama, and this is the best-evidenced example: the museum, not merely the book, names him as a sitter.
images.nature: A 19th-century history painting — an invention, not a likeness. Which figure is Tycho rests on the museum's metadata and the depicted narrative (corroborated by Eller 1978, p. 43), not on physiognomy: at this scale no head carries a discriminator of either the engraved or the painted tradition, and no source documents Hansen's model.

whereabouts.summary: Hanging at Frederiksborg, Room 27.
whereabouts.tier: located (record-level page; the museum's 'afbildede personer' field names Brahe, Queen Sophie and Vedel)
whereabouts.note: A 154, the Stjerneborg nocturne, names NO sitters in the museum's record — confirmed by a direct fetch of its own page (frederiksborg.dk/kunstvaerk/a-154/), a thinner record with no cross-reference to A 153 — and no figure in it can be identified, so it is recorded here rather than as a separate depiction. The museum serves only a 210 × 202 px image of A 153 (nine size parameters tested, byte-identical); the high-resolution Commons surrogate on file is the sister version Hansen also painted (Bruun Rasmussen 2005; evidently Phillips, Loeb collection, 2026), not A 153.

images.label: Eckersberg's sketch, 1831 — the young Christian IV visiting Hven
images.maker: C. W. Eckersberg.

bounds.argument: The caption dates the related history painting to 1831 (diary: painting finished 23 March 1831; etchings May–June 1831; SMK KKS2591 inscribed May 1831). The sheet itself is undated: preparatory if the caption's 'til historiemaleri' framing is right (before March 1831), later if it belongs to the print campaigns, whose last documented drawing episode is 18 June 1842 (the block drawing for Flinch).

images.description: A pencil sketch by Eckersberg, captioned in 2006 as a study for his history painting of the young Christian IV visiting Tycho Brahe on Hven. The bearded man at the globe is the Tycho figure. Eckersberg treated the subject across a documented 1831–1842 series — a first sketch laid out 31 January 1831 (initially the gold-chain moment), the finished painting, an oil sketch, two etchings, and an 1842 woodcut design for the atlas to Ursin's survey of the graphic arts — and his treatment appears isolated in 19th-century Danish painting; whether this sheet is preparatory or derivative within the series is undetermined.
images.nature: A 19th-century invention. No claim to likeness.

whereabouts.summary: Attested at Frederiksborg on a single 2006 credit line (Fig. 2, p. 247). Characterised triple negative: the 2006 volume has no picture-credit apparatus (its back matter is a Litteraturliste only); absent from Frederiksborg's fully-enumerated published catalogue (~1,791 sitemap records) — which the museum itself states excludes its drawings holdings; absent from SMK (three etchings, zero drawings), from Weilbach, and from the demonstrably incomplete national aggregator (samlinger.slks.dk).
whereabouts.holder: Det Nationalhistoriske Museum på Frederiksborg (attested only)
whereabouts.tier: attested — one 2006 credit line, no inventory number, no reproduction located online
whereabouts.note: The reproduction is Fig. 2 on printed p. 247 — printed p. 245 carries Fig. 1, Heinrich Hansen's 1882 Vedel/Sophie painting, so prior citations of p. 245 for this sheet are wrong. The museum's public catalogue is a selection and does not publish its drawings (institutionally confirmed: the museum states its drawings and prints cannot be permanently exhibited). Beware an OCR trap: the caption reads 1831, which the corpus scan renders '18381'.

open_questions: Direct enquiry to Frederiksborg (info@frederiksborg.dk) for the sheet's inventory number, accession history, medium, and dimensions — the only remaining route from attested to located.
Is the sheet a preparatory drawing, or a transfer/derivative drawing of the print campaigns — including its relation to the 18 June 1842 block drawing for Flinch?
Consult Villadsen's 2009 edition of Eckersberg's diaries (print only) and Fischer 1983, Tegninger af C.W. Eckersberg.
Identify the 27 February 2018 auction of the 26 × 17 cm oil (probable Hannover no. 441; the house is login-gated on MutualArt).
Post-1992 whereabouts of the painting (Hannover no. 438) after Helge Pedersen.

images.label: The Levy memorial sheet — Tycho for children
images.maker: Published by A. Levy, Copenhagen — the sheet itself is imprinted 'Forlagt af A. Levy.' (two independent 600-dpi readings of the 2006 reproduction; 'Levison' is incompatible with the glyphs), but the firm is untraced in every reached Danish trade source: the name rests on the image alone.

bounds.argument: The sheet carries no date. The 2006 caption guesses 'måske 1901?' — with the question mark, which must be preserved; the guess is undefended in print, though it sits adjacent to the volume's ten pages of Prague-1901 material. Orthography and diction narrow nothing: 'ei' and 'smaae' are long-lived literary archaisms (ODS s.vv. 'ej', 'smaa'), and 'Uranienborg' is Tycho's own original name-form, used here as an antiquarian gesture. No publisher dates for any 'A. Levy' have been found in any consulted source, so the c. 1855 lower bound is conventional, not evidenced. The bounds remain wide for want of evidence.

images.description: A 'Historisk Mindeblad' — a historical memorial sheet for children — from the series 'Danske Billeder for smaae og store Börn', no. 3, both series line and number printed on the sheet itself. The sheet is a full 3×3 picture grid: a central column of an oval bust lettered TYCHO. BRAHE. * 14 December 1546 + 24 October 1601 (the lettering confirmed exact), a large Uranienborg elevation in a moated formal garden, and a six-line verse panel over a sleeping dog, flanked by eight uncaptioned genre vignettes — instruments, a pair of armillary spheres, women at a spinning wheel, garden and reading scenes, figures in Renaissance pastiche dress. The bust is bare-headed and corresponds to the standing type (aetatis 50), not the plumed-cap de Gheyn engraved type — a visual comparison only, with no intermediate print traced. The verse reads: 'I længst forsvundne Dage Uranienborg hist laae, / Paa Hveen, hvor Tycho Brahe op paa de Stjerner saae, / Saa riig, saa skjøn og pragtfuld den stod, som her Du seer, / Men ak! den sank i Gruset, nu Borgen er ei meer. / Vi gjemme kun dens Billed og Mindet om den Mand, / Som var og altid bliver en Stolthed for vort Land!' This is Tycho as schoolroom furniture: the point at which the engineered image had become a national children's story.
images.nature: A 19th-century popular derivative of the portrait tradition (the central bust follows the bare-headed standing type rather than the de Gheyn engravings). One physical sheet.

whereabouts.summary: Attested in Nationalmuseet's topographical archive on the museum's own 2006 statement; no live record found.
whereabouts.tier: attested — the 2006 caption only; the museum's collections database returns nothing
whereabouts.note: Mortensen 1946 does not cover the sheet — verified by exhaustive full-text search of the whole Cassiopeia 1946 volume (no hit for the sheet, the series, or any Levy), not merely inferred from his scope — and it cannot be the source of the caption's '1901?'. Mortensen also published a 1949 iconography survey, not yet checked.

open_questions: Identify 'A. Levy' in the Danish trade record — Kraks/T. Krak Vejviser c. 1855–1905, Dansk Bogfortegnelse, Dansk Boghandlertidende, and KB Småtrykssamlingen; test other Levy first names, since 'A.' alone is thin.

Run the Mediestream sweep: the verse lines in full text (a terminus post quem for the poem independent of the publisher question), Copenhagen papers Oct–Dec 1901 for advertised Tycho commemorative sheets, and the Nationaltidende 23.9.1901 article itself.
Bundle the ATA enquiry — physical sheet or photograph only? journal/inventory number? high-resolution scan? — into the pending Uraniborg-drawings e-mail.
Trace the intermediate 19th-century print behind the bare-headed oval bust, which would give an independent terminus post quem.
Check Mortensen's 1949 iconography survey, and whether any register of Alfred Jacobsen's 'Danske Billeder' documents a no. 3.

images.label: The full-figure watercolour at Strahov — the standing Tycho with a sextant
images.date: c. 1598 – 1666; the drawing's date is open
images.maker: Unknown. Friis raises the possibility that it is by Philip Kilian, which would make it seventeenth-century and no witness to Tycho at all — 'Hvem Tegningen skyldes, vides ikke; maaske er den af Kilian.'

bounds.argument: The lower bound is the book it is bound into — a copy of the Progymnasmata that Tycho gave away, with his autograph dedication to Johann Zajíc von Hasenburk. But Friis warns that a drawing bound into a presented book need not be contemporary with the book: 'naar Vandfarvetegningen nu findes i en Bog, som Tyge Brahe har bortforæret, saa følger dog ikke heraf, at den er samtidig med Bogen.' The upper bound is Philip Kilian's engraving in Historia coelestis (Augsburg: Utzschneider, 1666, ed. Albert Curtz as 'Lucius Barrettus'), which the drawing either precedes as its model or follows as a derivative — Friis's 'Vienna 1657' imprint for the plate is refuted, and no documented 1657 issue exists. The 1881 report is now read at the source rather than through Friis: Vierteljahrsschrift der Astronomischen Gesellschaft 16, p. 273, in the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek's digitisation.

images.description: A watercolour on parchment, in folio, bound in front of a copy of the Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata at Strahov — a second book Tycho presented to the same Bohemian magnate who received the Strahov Mechanica. The composition is unlike every other painted Tycho: a full-length standing figure on a plinth, leaning on a sextant, in a beret and a long cloak reaching to the base, the whole reading as the depiction of a statue rather than of a man. Professor Šafařík distributed photolithographs of it to those present at the astronomical society's Strasbourg meeting in 1881, describing it as the only original portrait of Tycho in Prague.
images.nature: Genuinely open, and the interesting question about it. Friis observes that the photolithograph agrees with Philip Kilian's engraving in Historia Coelestis (ed. Albert Curtz as 'Lucius Barrettus', Augsburg 1666) in both form and size so closely that the drawing may be the very model for the plate — but equally it may be after it, or by Kilian himself. Friis's own view is that the ultimate original behind both is de Gheyn's engraving. Šafařík's 1881 description of it as 'the only original portrait of Tycho in Prague' should not be relied on. A first comparison against Kilian's plate (made here, at matched figure height) confirms beyond doubt that the two are the same composition, in the same direction, with the same pose, instrument, beret, ruff, fur-lined cloak and stance. It does not settle direction: the engraving is more elaborate throughout — a larger plume, a more structured beret, a more articulated instrument — which is what one expects both of an engraver elaborating a simpler model AND of a line engraving beside a halftone of a watercolour. The question stays open. The pair has since been run through the house vorlage protocol, which adds one datum: the two are same-sense. Under the house mirror rule — six of six calibrated Netherlandish painting-to-engraving pairs reverse — a same-sense pair leans against the watercolour having served as a face-up-traced production model for the plate. Two caveats keep this a lean rather than a verdict: the observation is made on the 1901 wrapper, whose undocumented reproduction chain may itself flip orientation; and the rule is calibrated on a different workshop tradition seventy to eighty years earlier — Kilian's own transfer practice is undocumented, and blackened-verso and counterproof transfers print same-sense. The direction question thus leans against Friis's model reading without being settled.

whereabouts.summary: At Strahov, in a presentation copy of the Progymnasmata — a different book from the Strahov Mechanica.
whereabouts.holder: Strahovská knihovna, Královská kanonie premonstrátů na Strahově
whereabouts.tier: attested — Friis and the Vierteljahrsschrift der Astronomischen Gesellschaft (1881); no live Czech record reached
whereabouts.note: Distinct from the Strahov Mechanica. Both were presented by Tycho to Jan Zbyněk Zajíc z Házmburka, so the same recipient holds two Tycho presentation volumes, each carrying a watercolour portrait — and the two portraits are of different types. Status is 'untraced', not 'extant': the object's survival rests on the 1881 report and nothing later. A third independent silence has since been added: Boldan & Vackářová, Bibliotheca astronomica (Národní knihovna ČR, 2024), pp. 88–91 — a Strahov-focused Tycho chapter — illustrates only the Mechanica and returns no trace of this Progymnasmata volume, the strongest of the three silences, 143 years after the report. The same source gives the sibling Mechanica's current shelfmark, AG XI 56. The Strahov OPAC is Katalog Tritius (strahovskyklaster.tritius.cz), CAPTCHA-blocked to non-browser tools, and Manuscriptorium's results page is a JavaScript shell — the live-record check is therefore unexecuted, not negative. Friis's imprint for the Kilian engraving, 'Vienna 1657', is refuted — see the Kilian record.

conflicts.question: Is the drawing the model for Kilian's engraving, or a copy of it?
conflicts.positions: Model — Friis notes the photolithograph and the engraving agree in form and size so exactly that 'det maaske netop er denne Tegning, hvorefter Stikket er udført'. Derivative — the drawing may equally be by Kilian, in which case it postdates the plate in conception.
conflicts.status: unresolved, and it decides whether this is a lifetime object or a seventeenth-century one — the engraving is now recorded separately as icon-kilian-standing, with its plate at Wellcome 1357i, so the comparison Friis made by eye can be made properly as soon as an image of the watercolour is obtained. Dreyer endorses the model reading twice — Tycho Brahe (1890), printed p. 264, the sole occurrence in the book (the circulating citation 'notes p. 288' is an error), and again, unhedged, in his preface to Opera Omnia X (1923, via Meddelelser fra Ole Rømers Venner 14/1, 2006, p. 31) — but both endorsements root in the single 1881 Šafařík report: endorsement, not independent evidence. The same-sense finding recorded under nature leans against the model reading, carried with its two caveats.

conflicts.question: Does the Studnička wrapper reproduce the watercolour, or Kilian's engraving?
conflicts.positions: For the watercolour: the wrapper has the plain slab and the facsimile signature, which are Friis's stated differentiators, and a facsimile signature is a positive feature that cannot be produced by cropping an engraving. Against certainty: the wrapper is a 1901 halftone, and Studnička nowhere says what he reproduced.
conflicts.status: well-supported but with undocumented chain of custody — Friis's differentiators (plain slab, facsimile 'Tycho Brahe') are his own observations from a copy of the 1881 photolithograph in hand, absent from the Vierteljahrsschrift minutes he quotes, and neither feature can be produced by cropping or retouching the engraving; whether the wrapper prints from the 1881 plate or a fresh reproduction of the same original remains undocumented

open_questions: Is Studnička's wrapper a print from Šafařík's 1881 plate, or a fresh 1901 reproduction of the same original? Studnička's text is silent.

Studnička's catalogue documents the Strahov MECHANICA copy in detail but never mentions this Progymnasmata volume or the 1881 episode. The silence is now partially explained: his item C.I footnote borrows an illustration from a Progymnasmata, 1603, at Strahov, so a copy was accessible to him in 1900–01 — which weakens any inference that the volume had left Strahov by 1901 — and his catalogue's scope (ownership-relics of Tycho's own library) plausibly excludes a presentation gift, though that genre explanation is a candidate reading, not established. Whether the accessible copy is the same volume is unknown.

No sighting of the Progymnasmata volume after 1881 has been located; Boldan & Vackářová's Strahov-focused Tycho chapter (2024) adds a third independent silence. Whether it is still at Strahov is unverified — the live-record check against Katalog Tritius (CAPTCHA-blocked to non-browser tools) and Manuscriptorium (a JavaScript shell to non-browser tools) remains unexecuted, not negative.

The Mechanica census records a Strahov copy; the Progymnasmata census (brahe-progymnasmata-1602, 9 copies) has no Strahov/Hasenburk copy. This volume is untracked in the census layer and warrants a copy-addition proposal — now staged with the 1603 issue, per Studnička's C.I footnote, identified as the attested Strahov host edition; whether that accessible copy is the Hasenburk volume is unknown.
Compare the wrapper against Kilian's plate at higher resolution than a 1901 halftone allows — the direction of dependence is still open, and the halftone is too coarse to settle it.
images.image_credit: The standing Tycho, reproduced on the printed wrapper of F. J. Studnička, Prager Tychoniana (Prague: Verlag der kön. böhm. Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften, 1901). The wrapper shows the two features Friis gives as diagnostic of the photolithograph rather than of Kilian's engraving: a plain rectangular slab in place of an architectural pedestal, and the name 'Tycho Brahe' in facsimile beneath the figure instead of an engraver's signature. Whether the wrapper prints from Šafařík's 1881 plate or from a fresh reproduction of the same Strahov original is not documented.

images.label: Kilian's standing Tycho (1666) — a whole body invented around a borrowed head
images.maker: Philip Kilian (Augsburg, 1628–1693, son of Wolfgang Kilian), signed at the foot of the pedestal 'Philip Kilian sculps.'

bounds.argument: The lower bound comes from the plate's companion. The same gathering carries a double-page frontispiece by the same hand, signed identically, showing four Habsburg emperors with putti holding banderoles — PARAVIT, …PAVIT, RECEPIT, PVBLICAVIT — a programme that culminates in the reigning emperor under whom the book was published, Leopold I. Leopold was not elected until 18 July 1658, so no plate in that gathering can predate it. The upper bound is publication: Historia Coelestis, Augsburg, Simon Utzschneider, 1666.

images.description: Tycho at full length, standing on an architectural pedestal and leaning on a large triangular sighting instrument, in a plumed beret and a fur-lined cloak falling to the plinth. Dreyer and Friis both call the instrument a sextant, but no graduated arc is visible in either examined impression; the open frame more nearly resembles Tycho's parallactic-ruler (triangulum) type, and no positive match to any Mechanica plate has been made — the identification is uncertain. (The small mark at the frame's base is joinery — a peg and foot-bracket, with a matching pivot-pin at the apex — not a letter or plate-mark.) The whole composition reads as the depiction of a statue rather than of a living man, and that is roughly what it is: a monument invented sixty-five years after his death, for the first printed edition of his observation logs.
images.nature: A posthumous invention, and demonstrably a composite. The pedestal inscription is not Kilian's: it is transcribed from de Gheyn's engraved portrait — a bust, in a different composition — with a single lexical substitution, instrumentorumque Astronomicorum … dispositorum for de Gheyn's Machinarumque Astronomicarum … dispositarum. Everything else runs word for word, including 'Aetatis suæ anno 40. Anno Dñi. 1586 compl.' THE CONSEQUENCE MATTERS: the 1586 and the age of 40 on this plate are inherited text, not evidence about the standing figure. Anyone dating this portrait type from its own inscription is dating a borrowing. Direct examination of two impressions shows every checkable costume element reading the de Gheyn v2 scheme — medal absent, beret worn and plumed, a single doubled chain, the gripping hand at the viewer's left — and none reading v1; but the v2 scheme is also attested in the drawing family and was the dominant circulating type, so this fixes the costume vocabulary, not which carrier Kilian copied. Prandtl (1901) moreover reads the nose-prosthesis on this plate — a feature present in neither de Gheyn state — which, if his reading holds, would mean the head is not a pure de Gheyn transfer; the reading is unconfirmed at available resolution and is carried as Prandtl's, not as observed fact.

whereabouts.summary: An edition multiple, in copies of the 1666 Historia Coelestis, and separately catalogued as a print.
whereabouts.tier: located (record-level catalogue page, IIIF at 2123 × 3272, Public Domain Mark)
whereabouts.note: Burgess, Portraits of Doctors & Scientists in the Wellcome Institute (1973), no. 405.9. Further impressions: the Royal Danish Library copy of the book, Fol. Astr. 35430, digitised at leaf 18; and a copy in the trade photographed at high resolution, whose plate agrees with the Wellcome impression in every detail including the signature — same plate, same state. The 1672 Ratisbonae cancel-title reissue carries the portrait plate: the K10plus/VD17 collation gives '[1] Portr. (Kupferst.)' with a note identifying the edition as a reprint of Augsburg 1666 (the printer is given as Emmrich in that single record, uncorroborated). A further impression: Royal Society, MS/648, Turnor Collectanea Newtoniana, plate 273 × 174 mm (pictures.royalsociety.org/image-rs-17166). Caution: Wellcome's own catalogue dates the print 1586, straight from the borrowed plinth inscription — an institutional instance of this record's inherited-text warning.

conflicts.question: Vienna 1657 or Augsburg 1666?
conflicts.positions: Friis cites the plate as belonging to 'Historia coelestis … Wien 1657, i Folio'. Two distinct printings exist and he has conflated them: a small pilot volume, Sylloge Ferdinandea, with a 1656 title-page and a colophon naming David Hautt at Vienna in 1657, containing only the preface, Liber Prolegomenon and the 1582 observations; and the full Augsburg 1666 folio, which alone carries the three large plates. Mortensen 1946 perpetuates Friis's Vienna-1657 label in his p. 138 prose ('i Historia coelestis, Wien 1657') while his own table at p. 80 correctly gives 'P. Kilians Stik 1666' — the error has a documented transmission chain, Friis → Mortensen.
conflicts.status: settled against Friis, twice over: the pilot volume has no such plates, and the Leopold I argument makes 1657 chronologically impossible. Cite Augsburg 1666.

conflicts.question: Is the Strahov watercolour Kilian's model, or a copy after his plate?
conflicts.positions: Strahov held two distinct Tycho watercolours, routinely conflated: one in the Mechanica presentation copy (recorded by Biela in 1824; today AG XI 56) and one in a Progymnasmata copy, published in photolithograph by Šafařík in 1881 — only the second is in dispute here. Friis noted that the photolithograph agrees with this engraving in form and size so exactly that the drawing may be the very model — but added that it may equally be by Kilian himself. One asymmetry is suggestive rather than decisive: the watercolour reportedly shows a plain rectangular slab with 'Tycho Brahe' in facsimile beneath the figure, where the engraving has a full architectural pedestal carrying the borrowed inscription; adding a pedestal and importing an inscription is ordinary engraver's elaboration, stripping one back is not what a copyist usually does. Against the model reading now stands Friis's own Addenda (p. 420): Kraus and Studnička informed him privately that the photolithograph reproduced a drawn copy after Kilian's plate, which 'ikke mere findes der' — no longer found at Strahov. That testimony collides directly with Studnička 1901 (p. 60), which states in print that the Progymnasmata volume was preserved in the Strahov library; neither statement can be shown to supersede the other. Friis's own considered verdict, never retracted, is that drawing and engraving are independent siblings, both descending from de Gheyn — a judgment resting on the recurring inscription, that is on textual, not compositional, evidence. A final caution gates all prior comparisons: the reproductions in Studnička 1901 (pp. 44–48) are anchored, by Friis's Addenda and independently by Norlind's Mechanica census, to the Mechanica watercolour, not the disputed Progymnasmata one — so every side-by-side comparison made from that surrogate is provisional.
conflicts.status: still open, but rebalanced: documented testimony — Kraus and Studnička via Friis's addendum, and Studnička 1901's silence on the watercolour among his catalogued genuine Tychoniana — now leans against Strahov-as-model, without reaching dispositive: the reversal is method-less hearsay about an object already missing when it was reported, and collides with Studnička's own printed 'preserved'. The question still decides whether the Strahov watercolour is a lifetime object or a seventeenth-century one.
